common_mistakes: Confusing circular, the advertisement, with circle, the shape, when talking about store flyers.
Using circular to mean roundabout for routes, when circuitous is more accurate.

circular.etymology: From Middle English *circuler*, *circuleer*, *circulere*, from Old French *circulier*, from Late Latin *circularis*, from Latin *circulus*, diminutive of *circus* (“ring”).

senses.definition: A group of people all descended from a common ancestor, in fact or belief, especially when the exact genealogies are not known.
Any group defined by family ties with some sort of political unity.
A group of players who habitually play on the same team in multiplayer games.
A group of badgers.

core.definition: A large group of families who share a common ancestor and often a family name, loyalty and traditions.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short 'a' as in 'cat' and end firmly with 'n'. Learners sometimes add a vowel before the final 'n' or lengthen the vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing family loyalty. It can sound exclusive or negative when describing closed groups, and it carries a distinct historical association in the United States.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use clan for Scottish families, tribal groups, large extended families and informal groups with strong loyalty. In casual speech, people might say 'our clan' jokingly for a big family gathering. Because of its association with the Ku Klux Klan in American history, be careful with capital letters and context, and avoid the word in discussions of hate groups.

distinctions.note: Tribe usually refers to a larger society with shared language and territory, while clan is a smaller kinship group within it.
Family is the everyday word for parents and children, while clan is larger and includes extended relatives.

examples.everyday: Our whole clan gets together every Thanksgiving at my aunt's house.
examples.professional: The consulting team operates like a clan, so newcomers take a while to be accepted into the inner circle.
examples.analytical: Anthropologists debate whether the clan is a real kinship unit or a social construct imposed by outside observers.

nuance.analogy: A clan is like a large extended tree whose branches share one root.
nuance.etymology: From Scottish Gaelic clann, meaning children or offspring, from Old Irish cland.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long 'a' or adding an extra vowel before the 'n'.
Using clan to mean any small group of friends, when it suggests a larger, family-based group.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew mishpachah, family, clan or kinship group. Joshua 7:14-18 describes Israel being brought forward by tribes, clans and households to identify Achan. Judges 6:15 has Gideon describe his clan as the weakest in Manasseh.

clan.etymology: Irish *clann* (“offspring, children of the family”) and *clann*, both from *cland*, borrowed from *plant*, itself borrowed from Latin *planta* (“shoot, offspring”).

senses.definition: A curved, pointed, horny projection on each digit of the foot of a mammal, reptile, or bird.
A foot equipped with such.
The pincer (chela) of a crustacean or other arthropod.
A mechanical device resembling a claw, used for gripping or lifting.
A human fingernail, particularly one extending well beyond the fingertip.
The act of catching a ball overhand.
A tree with one internal vertex and three leaves.
A slender appendage or process, formed like a claw, such as the base of petals of the pink.
To scratch or to tear at.
To use the claws to seize, to grip.
To use the claws to climb.
To perform a claw catch.
To move with one's fingertips.
To relieve an uneasy feeling, such as an itch, by scratching (someone or something); hence, to flatter or humor (someone); to court, to fawn on.
To rail at, revile, or scold (someone or something).
To do (something) quickly.

core.definition: A sharp, curved, pointed nail on the toe of an animal such as a cat, bird or lobster.

pronunciation.tip: Use the open back vowel of 'law' and end with a soft 'w' sound. Do not add an 'r' after the vowel, since the word is not rhotic in this position.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses, but it can suggest danger, aggression or sharpness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use claw for cats, birds, bears and crabs, and in everyday talk about pets, such as trimming the cat's claws. Lobster claws are the large pincers, so context matters. Americans also use claw as a verb meaning to scratch or grab at something.

distinctions.note: A nail is on a human finger or toe, while a claw is curved and sharp on an animal's toe.
A talon is a claw of a bird of prey, especially an eagle or hawk, while claw is the general term.

examples.everyday: Be careful when you pick up the cat, because her claws can scratch your arms.
examples.professional: The gripper claw on the warehouse robot failed on the third test cycle and needs a new sensor.
examples.analytical: In the fable, the fox's claws stand for the unrestrained ambition of those who hold power.

nuance.analogy: A claw is like a built-in tool that an animal carries on its feet, always ready to grip.
nuance.etymology: From Old English clawu, from a Proto-Germanic root meaning to claw or to grasp.
common_mistakes: Adding an 'r' sound after the vowel, as in 'klor'.
Confusing claw with clay, which has a completely different vowel and meaning.

claw.etymology: From Middle English *clawe*, from Old English *clawu*, from Proto-Germanic **klawō*.

senses.definition: The lower-fare service whose passengers sit in this part of the airplane or train; economy class.
The part of a commercial passenger airplane or train reserved for those paying the lower standard fares; the economy section.
senses.example: We couldn't afford the good tickets, so we spent the flight crammed in coach.

senses.definition: A trainer or instructor.
senses.example: football coach

senses.definition: A wheeled vehicle, generally pulled by a horse.
The forward part of the cabin space under the poop deck of a sailing ship; the fore-cabin under the quarter deck.
Via the part of a commercial passenger airplane or train reserved for those paying the lower standard fares; via the economy section.
senses.example: John flew coach to Vienna, but first-class back home.

senses.definition: To instruct; to train.
senses.example: She has coached many opera stars.

senses.definition: To train.
To study under a tutor.
To travel in a coach (sometimes coach it).
To convey in a coach.

core.definition: A person who trains and instructs an athlete or team, or who gives guidance to improve someone's skills or performance.

pronunciation.tip: Use one syllable with a long o sound and a 'ch' at the end. Do not add a 't' sound before the 'ch', and do not pronounce the 'a' as a separate vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests support, skill, and encouragement, and in American culture it is a respected role, although coach can also refer to economy class on flights or trains.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use coach very commonly for sports trainers, such as a basketball or soccer coach, and also for professional coaching in business or life. In a flight, 'coach' means economy class, and Americans say 'I'm flying coach' or 'an upgrade from coach.' When someone says 'I'm your coach,' it usually sounds warm and supportive rather than bossy.

distinctions.note: A teacher focuses on academic knowledge in a school setting, while a coach focuses on improving performance through practice and feedback.
Trainer is common for fitness or animals and can sound more physical or mechanical, whereas coach often sounds more strategic and supportive.

examples.everyday: My daughter's soccer coach is great, she makes every kid feel like they're improving.
examples.professional: Our manager hired an executive coach to help her prepare for the leadership role.
examples.analytical: The coach's role is ambiguous in the literature: it can mean instruction, support, or accountability.

nuance.analogy: Like a GPS for a runner: it does not run the race, but it shows the route and corrects your course.
nuance.etymology: From Hungarian kocsi, meaning a carriage, named after the village of Kocs; the sense of a trainer comes from the idea of carrying someone to their goal.
common_mistakes: Saying 'coach' for a bus, which in American English is a bus or a motorcoach, while 'coach' means economy class on planes or trains.
Pronouncing the vowel as in 'cot' rather than the long o in 'coach'.

coach.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *coche*, from German *Kutsche*, from *kocsi*, a clipping of "kocsi szekér".

conversation.text: The coach called a timeout to talk to the players.
He's been the head coach for ten years.
She coaches her daughter's soccer team.
We flew coach, and my knees were jammed against the seat.

senses.definition: The process of precisely formulating a statement, such as a code of laws.
senses.example: The task force spent months on the codification of their mandate.

senses.definition: The act or result of arranging something into a code; the act of setting down a body of knowledge in a systematic way.

core.definition: The act of arranging laws, rules, or knowledge into a complete, organized system, usually written down in a formal way.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the '-ca-' syllable, which is pronounced 'KAY', and the ending is 'shuhn'. Many learners stress the first syllable instead, which makes the word sound off.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests order, clarity, and authority, but can imply rigidity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use codification in law, policy, and academic writing, as in 'the codification of federal tax rules.' In casual talk, people say 'writing it down' or 'making it official.' It is a heavy, formal word, so 'documenting' is often more natural in a meeting.

distinctions.note: Documentation is any written record of how something works, while codification is a more formal arrangement into rules or a systematic code.
Standardization makes practices uniform across groups, while codification writes existing rules or knowledge into a formal system that may or may not standardize practice.
Legislation creates new laws, while codification gathers existing laws into one organized body without changing their substance.

examples.everyday: My friend said the new company handbook is just a codification of stuff people already do.
examples.professional: The team's codification of coding standards will save us from arguing about style in every review.
examples.analytical: The codification of customary law into written statutes often reshapes whose interpretations count as authoritative.

nuance.analogy: Codification is like turning a family's unwritten habits into a recipe book so anyone can follow them.
nuance.etymology: From code, from Latin codex meaning book, plus -fy from Latin facere meaning to make, with the suffix -ation.
common_mistakes: Using codification for a casual list; it implies a formal, systematic arrangement.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the '-ca-' syllable.
Confusing codification with codex or code; the noun is built from the verb codify.

senses.definition: To examine diverse documents and so on, to discover similarities and differences.
senses.example: The young attorneys were set the task of collating the contract submitted by the other side with the previous copy.

senses.definition: To assemble something in a logical sequence.
To sort multiple copies of printed documents into sequences of individual page order, one sequence for each copy, especially before binding.
senses.example: Collating was still necessary because they had to insert foldout sheets and index tabs into the documents.

senses.definition: To admit a cleric to a benefice; to present and institute in a benefice, when the person presenting is both the patron and the ordinary; followed by to.
senses.example: (Can we add an example for this sense?)

core.definition: To gather information or documents from several sources and arrange them in order so they can be compared.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, LAYT, with a reduced schwa at the start. In the printing sense some Americans say KOH-layt, but the comparison and data sense is kuh-LAYT.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a careful, methodical process without any emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: In offices and data work, Americans use collate for combining and ordering survey responses, records or printed pages before binding or analysis. In casual speech, people more often say put together or sort. A typical request is 'Can you collate these reports before the meeting?'

distinctions.note: Compare focuses on finding similarities and differences, while collate also includes gathering and arranging the material in order.
Compile means gathering material into a new whole, such as an anthology; collate emphasizes checking and sequencing existing items.

examples.everyday: Can you collate these printouts before we staple them, so the pages are in order for everyone?
examples.professional: I need to collate the survey responses from all three regions before Thursday's review, because the formats are different.
examples.analytical: The historian collated the surviving letters to reconstruct a timeline that none of the individual sources could provide.

nuance.analogy: To collate is like sorting a shuffled deck of cards into order so you can see which cards match and which are missing.
nuance.etymology: From Latin collatus, past participle of conferre, to bring together or compare, from com- 'together' and latus, the past participle of ferre 'to bear'.
common_mistakes: Confusing collate with correlate, which means showing a statistical relationship.
Using collate for ordinary sorting in casual speech, where put together or sort is more natural.

collate.etymology: From Latin *collātus*, perfect passive participle of *conferō*, see *-ate*.

senses.definition: A person who or thing that collects, or which creates or manages a collection.
senses.example: She is an avid collector of nineteenth-century postage stamps.

senses.definition: A person who is employed to collect payments.
senses.example: She works for the government as a tax collector.

senses.definition: A mafioso whose task is to collect protection money from small businesses.
The amplified terminal on a bipolar junction transistor.
A compiler of books; one who collects scattered passages and puts them together in one book.
A major sewer which collects sewerage from a number of smaller branch sewers.
One holding a Bachelor of Arts in Oxford, formerly appointed to superintend some scholastic proceedings in Lent.

core.definition: A person or thing that gathers and keeps items, or a person whose job is to collect money that is owed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable 'LEK'. The final '-or' is the American 'er' sound, a rhotic reduced vowel, so do not pronounce it as 'or' in 'door'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In debt contexts it can feel threatening; in hobby contexts it is positive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'collector' for a hobbyist who gathers stamps, art, or antiques, and for a debt collector, a person or agency paid to recover money owed. Debt collectors are often disliked, so 'a collector called me' usually sounds negative. In the Bible, 'tax collector' is the key term, and Americans will hear it in church.

distinctions.note: A collector acquires and owns items for personal interest or profit; a curator manages, displays, and cares for items on behalf of a museum or institution.
A gatherer picks or harvests things directly from nature or a field; a collector accumulates items, often by purchase or deliberate search.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a serious baseball card collector, and he keeps everything in plastic sleeves.
examples.professional: The collections team is reviewing accounts that the outside collector has flagged as overdue.
examples.analytical: Matthew's Gospel names a tax collector as a disciple, which challenges the assumption that the faithful should keep their distance from people who cooperate with empire.

nuance.analogy: A collector is like a squirrel storing nuts for winter: it gathers and holds onto things it values.
nuance.etymology: From Latin collector, one who gathers, from colligere, to gather together.
common_mistakes: Using 'collector' for a person who simply saves things casually; Americans say 'collector' only for someone with a deliberate, organized hobby.
Pronouncing the final 'or' as 'or' rather than the reduced American 'er'.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Gospels, the tax collector, Greek telones, is a Jewish man who collected taxes for Rome and was often seen as a traitor. In Matthew 9:9-10 (RSV), Jesus calls Matthew, a tax collector, to follow him, and then eats with tax collectors and sinners. In Luke 19:1-10, Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, is changed by Jesus and gives back what he took unfairly. Matthew 10:3 lists Matthew among the twelve apostles.

collector.etymology: Middle English *collectour*, from Anglo-Norman *collectour*, from Late Latin *collēctor*, from Latin *colligō* (“to gather together”).

senses.definition: To recover consciousness after fainting etc.
senses.example: She came to with the aid of smelling salts.

senses.definition: To total; to amount to.
senses.example: so how much does that come to?; the bill comes to £10 each

senses.definition: To reach; to arrive at.
senses.example: come to an end; come to a conclusion; come to an agreement; come to a halt

senses.definition: To seek help from.
senses.example: You can always come to me when you're feeling sad.

senses.definition: To devote attention to in due course; to come around to.
senses.example: I'll come to your question in a minute.

senses.definition: To befall; to happen to; to come upon.
senses.example: I pray no harm will come to you.

senses.definition: To regard or specifically pertain to.
senses.example: He's the best when it comes to detective fiction.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see come,‎ to.
To stop a sailing vessel, especially by turning into the wind. See also come about.

core.definition: To regain consciousness after fainting, being knocked out, or falling asleep briefly. Also, to add up to a total amount.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on COME, and TO is weak, so it sounds like 'kum-tuh' in fast speech. Do not stress the second word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The fainting sense can sound alarming in a medical situation, but the phrase itself is calm and matter-of-fact.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say that someone 'came to' after fainting, usually followed by 'on the floor' or 'in the ambulance', and 'came to' is common in first aid and hospital talk. For totals, Americans say 'The bill came to eighty dollars' in restaurants and stores, which is more natural than 'add up to' in casual speech.

distinctions.note: Wake up refers to leaving sleep, while come to refers to recovering consciousness after fainting or a blow to the head.
Add up to is slightly more informal and emphasizes the sum of separate parts, while come to is a neutral, everyday way to state a total.

collocations: came to a few minutes later

examples.everyday: He fainted in the kitchen, but he came to after a minute and said he was fine.
examples.professional: The vendor invoices for the cloud migration came to almost forty thousand dollars more than we planned.
examples.analytical: The patient was unconscious for several minutes, but she came to with no measurable neurological deficit.

nuance.analogy: Like a laptop screen that goes dark and then lights up again when you press a key.
nuance.etymology: From Old English cuman 'to come' combined with the preposition 'to', meaning toward a state or place.
common_mistakes: Using 'come back' for fainting; Americans say 'came to' after fainting, while 'come back' is for returning to a place or to health in a broader sense.
Saying 'the bill comes up to' instead of 'the bill comes to' for totals.

conversation.text: He fainted, but he came to after a few seconds.
When I came to, the nurse was holding my hand.
The bill came to two hundred dollars after insurance.

senses.definition: Compatible or consistent with another statement.

core.definition: Able to be true or to exist together without contradiction, so that two or more propositions are consistent with each other.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, as in 'possible,' which this word is built from. The given IPA put the stress on the first syllable, which is incorrect for this word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise philosophical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'compossible' almost only in philosophy and logic, especially in discussions of Leibniz and possible worlds. In everyday talk, people say 'compatible' or 'possible together.' In a seminar you could say 'jointly possible' to avoid the term.

distinctions.note: Consistent means not contradicting itself or others in general. Compossible specifically means able to be true or exist together in the same world.
Compatible is an everyday word for things that work together. Compossible is a technical term in philosophy and logic.

examples.everyday: I'm not sure those two plans are compossible, since I can't be in Boston and Denver on Friday.
examples.professional: Those two requirements are not compossible, so we need to prioritize one over the other.
examples.analytical: Leibniz held that a world is actual only if its states of affairs are mutually compossible.

nuance.analogy: Like two puzzle pieces that fit into the same picture without contradicting each other.
nuance.etymology: From Latin com- 'together' plus possibilis 'possible'; popularized in philosophy through Leibniz.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'KOM-puh-sable.'
Using it in everyday speech where 'compatible' would be the natural word.

senses.definition: Required; obligatory; mandatory.
senses.example: The ten-dollar fee was compulsory.

senses.definition: Having the power of compulsion; constraining.
senses.example: Such compulsory measures are limited.

senses.definition: Something that is compulsory or required.

core.definition: Required by a law, rule, or organization, so that you must do it.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PUL. In American speech the final -ory is usually a reduced 'uh-ree', with the r clearly pronounced. Learners often insert an extra vowel between the l and s or say 'sor-ee' at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It emphasizes requirement and obligation, which some people find restrictive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use compulsory in formal contexts like school rules, insurance, jury duty, and workplace training, as in 'compulsory training.' In everyday talk they usually say 'required' or 'mandatory.' Mandatory is especially common in American government and workplace language.

distinctions.note: Mandatory is more common in American English and is used for rules, policies, and requirements. Compulsory is more formal and often appears in education or law.
Optional means you can choose whether to do it. Compulsory means you have no choice.

examples.everyday: Sending your kids to school is compulsory in every state, so you can't just skip the first week.
examples.professional: Security training is compulsory for all staff, and the system will lock your account if you don't finish it by Friday.
examples.analytical: Mill argues that compulsory limits on personal liberty need strong justification, since they restrict the agent's own choices.

nuance.analogy: A compulsory rule is like a toll road: you may dislike it, but you have to pay to pass.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin compulsorius, from compellere, meaning 'to force'.
common_mistakes: Using compulsory for a strong personal urge, which is the job of compulsion or compulsive.
Saying 'compulsory' when an American speaker would prefer 'required' or 'mandatory' in everyday workplace talk.

senses.definition: An AI agent operating a computer as a person would: looking at the screen, moving the mouse and typing.

core.definition: An AI system's ability to operate a computer like a person, viewing the screen and controlling the mouse and keyboard.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on YOOS, which ends in an s sound because it is the noun form. Do not say it like the verb 'use', which ends in a z sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In AI discussions it describes a capability, and people note both its promise and its safety risks.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in AI product talk, tech news and developer discussions. It is a technical name for a capability, so you would hear it in a meeting about a new tool rather than in casual chat. A natural reply is 'Does it run in a sandbox?' or 'How reliable is it on multi-step tasks?'

distinctions.note: Computer use names the general capability of an AI to operate a computer, while a computer use tool is a specific product or software that provides that capability.
Automation is the broader idea of machines doing tasks without humans, while computer use specifically means an AI acting through a graphical screen like a person would.

examples.everyday: The new assistant can actually do computer use, so it can click through the website and fill in the form for you.
examples.professional: Our QA team is testing computer use agents to automate the repetitive form-filling in the claims system.
examples.analytical: Evaluating computer use shifts the question from whether a model writes good text to whether it can complete a multistep task in a real interface.

nuance.analogy: It is like giving an AI a pair of hands and eyes at a desk, so it works with the screen the way an assistant would.
nuance.etymology: 'Computer' comes from compute, and 'use' comes from Latin usus, 'employment'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the noun use with a z sound (yooz) instead of an s sound (yoos).
Using computer use to mean simply using a computer for everyday tasks; in AI it names a specific capability.

conversation.text: Computer use lets a model operate a desktop by reading screenshots and sending mouse clicks and keystrokes.
Computer use should run in an isolated virtual machine, never on a laptop with real credentials.
Computer use is still slow and error-prone on complex forms.

senses.definition: Happening at the same time; simultaneous.
Belonging to the same period; contemporary.
Acting in conjunction; agreeing in the same act or opinion; contributing to the same event or effect.
Joint and equal in authority; taking cognizance of similar questions; operating on the same objects.
senses.example: the concurrent jurisdiction of courts

senses.definition: Meeting in one point.
Running alongside one another on parallel courses; moving together in space.
Designed to run independently, rather than sequentially, using various mechanisms, such as threads, event loops or time-slicing.
One who, or that which, concurs; a joint or contributory cause.
One pursuing the same course, or seeking the same objects; hence, a rival; an opponent.
One of the supernumerary days of the year over fifty-two complete weeks; so called because they concur with the solar cycle, the course of which they follow.
One who accompanies a sheriff's officer as witness.

core.definition: Happening or existing at the same time as something else, often over an overlapping period.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KUR, the second syllable. The first syllable is a weak 'kuhn,' not 'kong.' The final -ent is a reduced 'uhnt.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes timing or agreement without praise or criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use concurrent in formal writing, legal and government contexts, and technical fields, as in 'concurrent sessions' or 'concurrent enrollment' in colleges. In casual speech they say 'at the same time.' As a noun, concurrent is rare and literary, meaning a contributing cause or a rival.

distinctions.note: Simultaneous means happening at exactly the same moment; concurrent allows overlapping events over a longer period.
Coincident describes events that happen to coincide by chance; concurrent describes events that overlap in time, often by design.

examples.everyday: I'm taking a community college class, so I'm doing a concurrent course while I work.
examples.professional: The team runs concurrent sprints, so two features can move forward at the same time.
examples.analytical: The historian argues that the two reform movements were concurrent but not causally connected.

nuance.analogy: Concurrent events are like two movies playing on overlapping schedules in the same theater.
nuance.etymology: From Latin concurrentem, the present participle of concurrere, 'to run together.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'concurrence,' which is a noun meaning agreement
Saying 'concurrent to' instead of 'concurrent with'
Using it in casual speech where 'at the same time' is more natural

concurrent.etymology: From Middle English *concurrent*, from Old French *concurrent*, from Latin *concurrēns*, present active participle of *concurrō* (“happen at the same time”), from *con-* (“with”) + *currō* (“run”).

senses.definition: A specialist in a given field whose opinion is highly valued, especially in one of the fine arts or in matters of taste.
senses.example: beer connoisseur

core.definition: A person with expert knowledge who is trusted to judge quality, especially in art, food, wine, or other matters of fine taste.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the last syllable, which sounds like 'sir' with a strong American r. The final -sseur is silent except for the r sound, so do not add an extra syllable like 'soor'.

nuance.connotation: Positive, because it praises someone's trained judgment. Calling yourself a connoisseur can sound pretentious, so it is safer to describe other people with it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use connoisseur for people who know good wine, coffee, art, or music, as in 'He's a real coffee connoisseur.' It is more formal than 'foodie' or 'expert' and sounds slightly elevated in casual talk. A natural modest reply to someone who praises your taste is 'I'm no connoisseur, I just know what I like.'

distinctions.note: An expert has broad knowledge or skill in a field; a connoisseur is valued specifically for fine judgment about quality and taste.
An aficionado is an enthusiastic fan who loves a pursuit; a connoisseur is someone whose judgment of quality is trusted.
Foodie is casual and popular in American speech; connoisseur is more formal and implies discriminating expertise.

examples.everyday: My brother is a real coffee connoisseur, so he'll tell you exactly where the beans came from.
examples.professional: Our design lead is a connoisseur of clean interfaces, and she can spot a bad layout in seconds.
examples.analytical: The critic presents himself as a connoisseur whose judgments reflect long study rather than mere personal preference.

nuance.analogy: A connoisseur is like a wine taster who can name the region and vintage from one sip.
nuance.etymology: From French connaisseur, from connaître 'to know', from Latin cognoscere.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -eur as a separate syllable, when it is silent.
Using connoisseur for any enthusiastic fan, when it implies trained judgment of quality.

connoisseur.etymology: Around 1705–1715, from French *connoisseur*, from the verb *connoître*.

senses.definition: Someone who conquers.

core.definition: A person or group that defeats others and takes control of land or people; someone who overcomes a difficulty.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. Americans say three syllables, with the middle one reduced to a schwa, so the word does not end in a double r sound.

nuance.connotation: Often neutral or admiring in historical or literary contexts; can sound grandiose or threatening when used of a real military leader.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use conqueror mostly in history, literature, and figurative speech, such as 'a conqueror of disease'. In everyday talk it is less common than winner or champion. It sounds dramatic if applied to ordinary achievements, so use it with humor or in a clearly figurative way.

distinctions.note: Winner is neutral and everyday; conqueror implies taking control of territory or overcoming a powerful opponent.
Victor is more formal and emphasizes the outcome of a contest; conqueror emphasizes the act of taking control.
Champion means the best in a competition or a defender of a cause; conqueror stresses domination or triumph over an obstacle.

collocations: Alexander the Great, a famous conqueror

examples.everyday: My grandfather jokes that he is the conqueror of every crossword puzzle in the newspaper.
examples.professional: The startup positioned itself as the conqueror of the legacy software market, though it still has to win customers.
examples.analytical: Paul calls the believer more than a conqueror, which reframes victory as participation in Christ's triumph rather than personal domination.

nuance.analogy: A conqueror is like the one who reaches the top of the mountain first and claims it; the word names the person at the summit of a struggle.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English conquerour, from Anglo-French conquerour, from conquerre (conquer).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a double r sound at the end, such as 'KAHNG-ker-ur-ur'.
Using conqueror as a general word for any winner in everyday contexts, where winner is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: The Bible uses the idea of a conqueror through the Greek nikaō and its related forms. Romans 8:37 describes believers as more than conquerors through Christ. Revelation 2:7 promises the one who conquers the right to eat from the tree of life. These passages present victory as coming through faith in Christ rather than through military force.

conqueror.etymology: From Middle English *conquerour*, from Old French *conquereor*, from *conquerre*.

senses.definition: A collection of goods to be sent, in transit or having been sent.
The act of consigning.

The sale of one's own goods (clothing, furniture, etc.) through a third-party vendor, in exchange for a portion of the sale price, and with the consigner retaining ownership of the goods until they are sold or abandoned.

core.definition: A store arrangement where goods are sold for an owner, who receives part of the price when they sell.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on SINE, the second syllable. The final -ment is a weak 'mint' without a strong t, so say it as 'munt'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests a smart, thrifty way to sell used items.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'consignment' for shops that sell used clothing, furniture, or art for the owner. You might say 'I bought this at a consignment shop', and the owner gets a cut of the price. For a shipment, Americans say 'shipment' or 'freight' more often. A natural reply is 'Oh, nice, do they take good stuff?'

distinctions.note: A thrift store usually buys donated items outright; a consignment shop pays the owner only after an item sells.
Secondhand is a general term; consignment specifically means the owner shares the sale price with the store.

examples.everyday: I sold my kids' old bikes at a consignment shop, and they gave me a good cut of the price.
examples.professional: We moved our inventory to consignment, so the vendor pays us only after each unit sells.
examples.analytical: Consignment shifts the risk of unsold goods from the retailer to the owner, which changes who bears the economic cost of market uncertainty.

nuance.analogy: Like renting a shelf in someone else's store, then paying them only when your item sells.
nuance.etymology: From consign plus -ment, from Latin consignare, 'to seal'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in consignment' instead of 'on consignment' in American English.
Using it for any kind of delivery; in the US 'consignment' usually means a shop arrangement or a batch of goods being sent, so 'shipment' is clearer in logistics.

conversation.text: She sells her designer bags at a consignment shop downtown.
I put my wedding dress on consignment, and it sold in a month.
That consignment store has great kids' clothes.

senses.definition: To deny the truth or validity of (a statement or statements).
senses.example: His testimony contradicts hers.

senses.definition: To oppose (a person) by denying the truth or pertinence of a given statement.
senses.example: Everything he says contradicts me.

senses.definition: To be contrary to (something).
To say things that conflict with each other.
senses.example: The prime minister contradicted herself during her speech.

core.definition: To say the opposite of what someone has said, or to show that a statement is false or inconsistent with the evidence.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the last syllable, DIKT, with a lighter secondary stress on KAHN. Americans flap the t in the middle, so it sounds like kahn-truh-DIKT rather than kahn-tuh-DIKT.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It can sound confrontational, so people often soften it in conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use contradict in ordinary conversation when someone disagrees with a fact, and in academic and professional settings to challenge a claim with evidence. Saying 'you're contradicting yourself' can sound accusatory, so soften it with 'I think that doesn't match what you said earlier'. A common polite reply is 'Actually, I think...' rather than a flat 'No.'

distinctions.note: Deny is about refusing to accept a claim, while contradict is about stating a claim that is the opposite of another.
Dispute means to argue against a claim, often with reasons, while contradict means to state the opposite directly.

examples.everyday: My brother always contradicts me about movie plots, but I'm pretty sure I'm right this time.
examples.professional: The second report contradicts the original estimate, so we need to recheck the sample data before presenting it.
examples.analytical: Her argument does not contradict Hume's premise but instead reframes it in terms of causal inference.

nuance.analogy: To contradict is like a second witness who says the opposite of the first witness, so one of them must be wrong.
nuance.etymology: From Latin contradicere, from contra, 'against', and dicere, 'to say'.
common_mistakes: Using 'contradict to' with a preposition; the verb takes a direct object, as in 'contradict him', not 'contradict to him'.
Confusing contradict with contract, which is pronounced differently and has an unrelated meaning.

contradict.etymology: Derived from Latin *contrādictus* (“contradicted”), the past participle of *contrādīcō* (“speak against”).

senses.definition: To decrease in temperature, activity, or temper.
senses.example: You are getting a little too angry; you need to cool off.

senses.definition: To cause to decrease in temperature, activity or temper.
senses.example: At first he was very angry, but his friends managed to cool him off.

senses.definition: To lose interest or enthusiasm [with on].
To be imprisoned.
senses.example: He's cooling off in the state pen.

senses.definition: To kill (someone).
To wait for a furor to die down; to hide during a police manhunt.
senses.example: After doing the job, he went to the safehouse to cool off.

core.definition: To become cooler in temperature, or to become calmer and less angry, often after heat or excitement.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'off', which is pronounced with an 'aw' vowel in General American, the same as 'caught'. The 'l' in 'cool' is clear and the words link smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It usually describes a temporary break from heat or anger and sounds friendly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use cool off when talking about weather, swimming or a hot day, such as 'Let's go cool off in the pool.' It is also used for anger, as in 'Give him time to cool off.' It is informal, so it fits well in conversation and texts but less well in formal reports.

distinctions.note: Cool down is slightly more general and can describe a process of lowering temperature; cool off is more conversational and often describes taking a break.
Lose interest is about attention or enthusiasm; cool off with an interest sense is informal and suggests a gradual drop in passion.

collocations: give someone time to cool off

examples.everyday: It's so hot today, let's go cool off at the lake.
examples.professional: Give the client a day to cool off before you reply to that angry email.
examples.analytical: The historian notes that the controversy only began to cool off once both sides stopped publishing rebuttals.

nuance.analogy: To cool off is like stepping out of the sun and into the shade: the heat does not vanish, but you feel relief.
nuance.etymology: Phrasal verb formed from cool and off.
common_mistakes: Confusing cool off with cool down in formal writing; both are fine in speech, but cool off sounds more casual.
Saying 'cool off myself' in a reflexive way; Americans usually say 'I need to cool off.'

conversation.text: Let's jump in the pool and cool off.
It finally cooled off a little after sunset.
He needs a few minutes to cool off after that argument.

senses.definition: In a corrupt manner.

core.definition: In a dishonest way, especially by accepting bribes or abusing a position of trust for personal gain.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable of the root, -RUPT-. The final -ly is pronounced 'lee,' and the first vowel is a reduced r-colored sound, not a clear 'or.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes wrongdoing by someone in power or trust, and it often appears in legal or political reporting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use corruptly mostly in legal or journalistic contexts, such as 'acting corruptly' in statutes about bribery or fraud. In everyday talk people say 'dishonestly' or 'on the take' instead. In the Bible, the word often describes deeds done in a way that is ruinous or wicked, which connects it to ethics.

distinctions.note: Dishonestly is general and everyday; corruptly implies abuse of public or trusted position, often with bribery.
Fraudulently focuses on deception for money; corruptly focuses on the abuse of power or trust.
Illegally means against the law in general; corruptly describes a specific kind of wrongdoing involving influence or bribes.

examples.everyday: My uncle says the city council members voted corruptly, but I haven't seen any proof yet.
examples.professional: The compliance memo warns that any employee who acts corruptly in vendor selection will be fired.
examples.analytical: The prophet denounces leaders who judge corruptly, arguing that justice is inseparable from faithfulness to God.

nuance.analogy: Acting corruptly is like a referee who secretly takes money from one team: the game still looks normal, but the outcome is rigged.
nuance.etymology: From Latin corrumpere, 'to spoil, destroy,' via Middle English corrupt.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a clear r and long o, as kor-UPT-lee, which sounds unnatural.
Using corruptly to mean 'rotten' or physically spoiled; it is about morality.
Confusing the adverb corruptly with the adjective corrupt in sentences like 'He corrupt the process.'
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew verb shachat, 'to ruin, corrupt,' appears in Genesis 6, where the earth is described as corrupt before God and humanity's ways are said to have corrupted the earth. Related ideas in the Old Testament describe leaders who judge corruptly by taking bribes and perverting justice. The New Testament uses the Greek word phtheiro, 'to ruin or destroy,' for the moral and physical ruin of people who turn from God. Genesis 6 and the prophetic critiques of unjust leaders are the key contexts for the adverb's sense.

senses.definition: Having matching boundaries; or, adjoining and sharing a boundary.
senses.example: New York's borough of Brooklyn and Kings County are coterminous.

senses.definition: Having the same scope, range of meaning, or extent in time.
Said of linked or related property leases that expire together.

core.definition: Having the same boundaries or the same extent in space, time, or meaning; sharing a common boundary.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, 'TUR', which is an r-colored vowel in American speech. The final syllables are weak and quick.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'coterminous' in legal, academic, and governmental writing, such as describing school districts or counties that share boundaries. It is rare in conversation and would sound stiff. In everyday speech, people would say 'the same' or 'shares a border with'.

distinctions.note: Adjacent means next to or near, without necessarily matching boundaries; coterminous means the boundaries match exactly or cover the same scope.
Contiguous means touching along a border, while coterminous emphasizes that two things have identical extent or edges.

examples.everyday: Our school district is pretty much coterminous with the town, so the boundaries match.
examples.professional: The new reporting region is coterminous with the sales territory, so we can combine the two dashboards.
examples.analytical: The author treats the concept of nation as coterminous with the concept of language, an identity that historians have repeatedly questioned.

nuance.analogy: Two coterminous maps are like two transparent sheets laid exactly on top of each other, with edges that line up perfectly.
nuance.etymology: From Latin con- meaning together, plus terminus meaning boundary or end.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as 'KOH-ter-minous'; the stress falls on the second syllable.
Using 'coterminous' to mean merely nearby; it requires shared or identical boundaries.

coterminous.etymology: From Latin *conterminus*, from *con-* (“with”) + *terminus* (“border, end”), equivalent to *co-* + *terminous*.

senses.definition: A person who lacks courage.
Cowardly.
Borne in the escutcheon with his tail doubled between his legs.

core.definition: A person who lacks courage and avoids danger, risk, or conflict because of fear.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a short, reduced 'erd' with an r-colored vowel. It is one syllable less than many learners expect, so avoid 'co-WARD.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling someone a coward is a serious insult in American culture, so use it carefully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'coward' to criticize someone who runs from a fight, avoids a hard conversation, or refuses a risk. It can sound harsh in polite company, so people often soften it with 'scared' or 'afraid.' As an adjective, 'cowardly' is more common in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Timid describes a naturally shy or nervous temperament, while coward is a harsher moral judgment about fleeing danger or duty.
Afraid describes a feeling of fear, while coward describes a person who acts from fear and lacks courage.
Chicken is informal slang for coward, often used playfully among friends rather than as a serious accusation.

examples.everyday: Don't be a coward, just ask her out already.
examples.professional: Calling the outage a known issue instead of owning it was pretty cowardly.
examples.analytical: Aristotle treats the coward as one who fears the wrong things at the wrong time and in the wrong way.

nuance.analogy: A coward is like a turtle that pulls into its shell at the first sign of trouble, staying safe but missing the chance to move forward.
nuance.etymology: From Old French coart, from coe 'tail,' from Latin cauda, suggesting a dog or animal that turns its tail and runs.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as two full syllables, 'co-ward,' instead of the reduced 'KOW-erd.'
Using 'coward' as a casual joke in serious business settings, where it can sound insulting.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew yare' means fearful or afraid, and the Greek deilos means cowardly or timid. Deuteronomy 20:8 has the officers ask whether any man is fearful and fainthearted, and they send him home so his fellows will not lose heart. Revelation 21:8 lists the cowardly among those excluded from the new Jerusalem. 2 Timothy 1:7 says God gave a spirit not of timidity but of power, love, and self-control.

coward.etymology: From Middle English *coward*, from Old French *coart*, *cuard*, from *coue* (“tail”), coe + *-ard*; *coue*, coe is in turn from Latin *cauda*.

senses.definition: A strong desire; yearning.

core.definition: A strong, persistent desire for something, especially a particular food or drink.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a short, unstressed vowel, not a long 'vee'. Avoid adding an extra syllable between the 'v' and the 'ng'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative: it describes a strong urge, often one that feels hard to resist, and it can be used for both food and deeper longings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use craving for everyday hunger-like urges, such as a craving for pizza or chocolate, and also for emotional or spiritual longing. You can say 'I have a craving for...' or 'I'm craving...' in casual speech. A natural reply is 'Me too' or 'What's bringing that on?'

distinctions.note: Desire is a broader and more general word, while a craving is more intense and often physical or habitual.
Longing suggests a wistful wish for something absent, often emotional, while a craving suggests a more urgent appetite.

examples.everyday: I have a serious craving for tacos right now, so let's go get some after work.
examples.professional: Our team has a craving for faster feedback, so we moved the model evaluations to nightly runs.
examples.analytical: Augustine describes a restless craving of the heart that no finite good can finally satisfy.

nuance.analogy: A craving is like a thirst that gets louder the longer it goes unanswered.
nuance.etymology: From Old English crafian, to ask for or demand.
common_mistakes: Saying 'craving of' instead of 'craving for' (for example, 'a craving for sweets', not 'a craving of sweets').
Pronouncing it with two stressed syllables or with a long second vowel.

craving.etymology: From Middle English *cravinge*, from Old English *crafing* (“claim, demand”); equivalent to *crave* + *-ing*.

conversation.text: I've been craving pizza all week.
I have a craving for something sweet after dinner.
Pregnant women sometimes have weird food cravings.
Late-night cravings are my biggest problem.
She's craving tacos tonight, so let's go to that food truck.

senses.definition: Being generated by only one element.
Able to be inscribed in a circle.
Characterized by, or moving in cycles, or happening at regular intervals; cyclical.
senses.example: The weather had a cyclic pattern of rain and sun.

senses.definition: Firing at its full cyclic rate.
Having chains of atoms arranged in a ring.
senses.example: Benzene and cyclohexane are both cyclic compounds.

senses.definition: Having parts arranged in a whorl.
The flight control used to control a helicopter's direction and rate of horizontal movement by tilting the lift vector of the helicopter's main rotor disk.

core.definition: Happening in regular cycles or repeating patterns; in mathematics, describing a group generated by a single element.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SY, and make the second syllable short and quick, with a clear /k/ at the end. Avoid adding an extra vowel between the /k/ and the final sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In mathematics it is a precise term; in general use it describes repetition without any judgment.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English people usually say 'cyclical' for repeating patterns, so 'cyclic' sounds more technical or formal. In mathematics, science, and chemistry, 'cyclic' is the standard term. Americans may use it in a meeting when they want a precise, technical tone.

distinctions.note: 'Cyclic' is the more technical and mathematical term, while 'cyclical' is the more common everyday adjective for repeating patterns.
Periodic means repeating at a fixed interval, while cyclic can describe a return to a starting point without a strictly fixed period.

examples.everyday: The weather here seems cyclic, with a rainy spell every spring.
examples.professional: Our forecasting model accounts for cyclic demand, so inventory rises and falls with the seasons.
examples.analytical: A cyclic group is one generated entirely by a single element, and that property makes its structure unusually transparent.

nuance.analogy: A cyclic pattern is like a carousel: you keep going around and come back to where you started.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kyklikos, 'circular', from kyklos, 'circle' or 'wheel'.
common_mistakes: Using 'cyclic' in casual speech where Americans would more naturally say 'cyclical'.
Adding an extra syllable, as in 'SY-kuh-lik', when the word has only two syllables.

cyclic.etymology: From French *cyclique* or its etymon Classical Latin *cyclicus*, from Ancient Greek *κυκλικός*.

senses.definition: The state of qualitative or quantitative pieces of information, usually described in aspects of completeness, conformity, consistency, accuracy, and integrity.

core.definition: How well data is complete, accurate, consistent, valid and timely enough to be trusted for its intended use.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KWAH, the first syllable of 'quality'. The middle syllable is a reduced 'luh', and the final 'ty' sounds like 'tee'. Americans often flap the t in 'data' and pronounce the 'l' lightly.

nuance.connotation: positive or neutral. Good data quality is valued, while poor quality is a problem to solve.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'data quality' in business and data science to describe whether information can be trusted. You will hear it in meetings about dashboards, reports or machine learning models. In casual talk, people might say 'the numbers are messy' or 'the data is bad' instead.

distinctions.note: Accuracy is only one dimension of data quality; data can be accurate yet incomplete or outdated.
Integrity focuses on whether data stays unaltered and consistent over its life, while quality is a broader measure of fitness for use.
Validation is a check performed when data enters a system, while data quality is the overall condition the checks aim to achieve.

examples.everyday: My mom's pharmacy app kept sending her wrong refill dates, and she joked that the data quality was terrible.
examples.professional: Before the model goes live, let's run data quality checks on the customer table, especially for missing zip codes and duplicate records.
examples.analytical: Data quality is not a single property but a judgment relative to purpose, since data adequate for one question may be unfit for another.

nuance.analogy: Like the freshness of ingredients: a recipe can be perfect, but if the produce is spoiled, the meal will fail.
nuance.etymology: 'Data' from Latin datum; 'quality' from Latin qualitas, from qualis, 'of what sort'.
common_mistakes: Using 'quality' as a count noun; it is usually uncountable, so say 'good data quality'.
Confusing it with 'data quantity'; more data is not necessarily better quality.

senses.definition: The act or art of declaiming; rhetorical delivery; loud speaking in public.
The public recitation of speeches as an exercise in schools and colleges.
A set or harangue; declamatory discourse.
Pretentious rhetorical display, with more sound than sense.
senses.example: mere declamation

core.definition: The act of speaking loudly and dramatically in public, or a forceful, overwrought speech delivered that way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MAY, the third syllable. The first -ation is reduced to 'shun', and the first syllables are short and quick.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, suggesting overwrought or theatrical speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use declamation in literary, historical and academic writing, and in speech contests or classical education. In everyday talk they would say speech, rant or a long lecture. It is a formal word, so use it with care in conversation.

distinctions.note: A declaration is a formal announcement of a fact or decision, while declamation is a style of delivery.
An oration is a formal public speech, while declamation emphasizes voice, force and performance.

examples.everyday: His declamation about the traffic lights went on for ten minutes.
examples.professional: The keynote was less a presentation than a declamation about the company's future.
examples.analytical: Quintilian treated declamation as essential training for the orator, joining voice, gesture and argument.

nuance.analogy: A declamation is a speech turned up to full volume and delivered like a performance.
nuance.etymology: From Latin declamatio, from declamare 'to practice speaking aloud'.
common_mistakes: Confusing declamation with declaration; they sound similar but mean different things.
Stressing the second syllable instead of MAY in dek-luh-MAY-shun.

declamation.etymology: From French *déclamation*, from Latin *declamatio*, from *declamo*; see *declaim*.

senses.definition: To take out of service or to render unusable.
senses.example: They decommissioned the ship after the accident.

senses.definition: To remove or revoke the commission of.
senses.example: After his arrest, the officer was decommissioned from the police force.

senses.definition: To remove or revoke the formal designation of.
senses.example: The state highway was decommissioned and reverted to local control.

core.definition: To take a system, machine or facility out of service permanently, or to make it unusable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MISH, and the first syllable has secondary stress. The last syllable is a reduced schwa, so say 'un', not 'on'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It sounds official and is used for systems, ships, reactors and software.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, decommission is common in engineering, IT and military contexts, where it means taking something permanently out of service. In everyday speech, people usually say take out of service, shut down or retire a system. In a meeting, say 'we'll decommission the old server next month' to sound precise and professional.

distinctions.note: Retire is more general and often used for people or equipment; decommission is the formal term for taking systems or facilities out of service.
Shut down can be temporary, while decommission usually means a permanent removal from service.

examples.everyday: The city is going to decommission the old water tower next year because it's no longer safe.
examples.professional: We need to decommission the legacy reporting service once all clients have migrated to the new API.
examples.analytical: Decommissioning a nuclear plant raises not only technical questions but also moral ones about who bears responsibility for the long-term waste.

nuance.analogy: Decommissioning a system is like retiring a veteran employee: the work is handed off, and then the position is closed for good.
nuance.etymology: From de- (removing) plus commission, from Latin committere, to entrust or commit.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as DEE-kuh-mish-un; the main stress is on MISH.
Using decommission as a synonym for turning off; it implies permanent removal from service.

senses.definition: Crossed; intersected; resembling a letter X.
(Can we verify this sense?) Consisting of two rising and two falling clauses, placed in alternate opposition to each other.
senses.example: a decussated period

senses.definition: Having anatomical structures or markings crossing each other, typically in an X shape or at right angles.
Having opposite leaves arranged alternately at right angles.
To form an X or to cross or intersect.

core.definition: To cross or intersect so as to form an X shape.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on KUH, the second syllable. The first syllable is a short, reduced i, and the ending is a clear ayt sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term used in botany, anatomy, and geometry.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use decussate almost only in scientific or technical writing, especially biology, botany, and anatomy. In everyday talk, they would say cross or intersect. Careful writers use it when they want to describe an X-shaped crossing precisely.

distinctions.note: Intersect is a general, everyday term for meeting and crossing lines or paths; decussate specifically means crossing in an X pattern.
Cross is common and flexible; decussate is precise and technical.
Transverse means lying across something at a right angle; decussate implies a crossing that forms an X.

examples.everyday: The two streets cross each other, almost like they decussate, right in the middle of town.
examples.professional: The diagram shows the nerve fibers decussate before reaching the thalamus, so the signal crosses sides.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the two traditions decussate at a single point, where their vocabularies overlap in an X pattern.

nuance.analogy: To decussate is like two people walking past each other in a crossing hallway, forming an X in the path they take.
nuance.etymology: From Latin decussatus, 'crossed in the form of an X,' from decussis, 'the X-shaped figure.'
common_mistakes: Using decussate in everyday conversation where cross is more natural.
Confusing it with decrease or decrepit because the spelling is similar.

decussate.etymology: The adjective is first attested in 1825, the verb in 1658.

senses.definition: The part of a swimming pool with relatively deep water.
A situation where expertise or experience is required.

core.definition: The deeper part of a swimming pool; figuratively, a difficult or unfamiliar situation requiring expertise.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word in this compound: DEEP END. The vowel in 'end' is short, as in 'bend'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly challenging; it can encourage or warn depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'deep end' for swimming pools in everyday speech, and for figurative situations, usually in phrases such as 'thrown into the deep end' or 'go off the deep end'. 'Go off the deep end' means to lose control or become unreasonably angry. Use it casually with friends and colleagues.

distinctions.note: The shallow end is the part of a pool with less water; the deep end is the opposite.
'Over one's head' describes being unable to understand or handle something; 'deep end' suggests being thrown into it, often with a learning curve.

examples.everyday: Our new manager threw me into the deep end on my first day, and I'm still catching up.
examples.professional: Since the senior analyst left, I've been in the deep end of the forecasting model without much documentation.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the reader is thrown into the deep end of the argument without any preliminary definitions.

nuance.analogy: Being in the deep end is like being handed a paddle on a choppy lake before you have learned to swim.
nuance.etymology: Combination of 'deep' and 'end', the words used in ordinary English for a pool's deeper section.
common_mistakes: Saying 'deep side' instead of 'deep end' for a pool.
Using 'go into the deep end' when the common idiom is 'thrown into the deep end'.

conversation.text: Don't go in the deep end until you can swim better.
The diving board is at the deep end of the pool.
They threw me in the deep end on my first day at work.

senses.definition: Serving, or suitable, for defense; defensive, defending.
In civil proceedings, the party responding to the complaint; one who is sued and called upon to make satisfaction for a wrong complained of by another.
In criminal proceedings, the accused.

core.definition: A person or organization against whom a lawsuit is brought or who is accused of a crime in court.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable, FEN. The final -ant is a reduced, unstressed syllable, so it sounds like 'dent', not 'dahnt'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a legal role and carries no judgment of guilt or innocence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use defendant for the party being sued in civil cases and for the accused in criminal cases. In a criminal case, many people say 'the accused' or 'the suspect' before charges, but 'defendant' once the case is in court. Do not use it for a witness or a plaintiff.

distinctions.note: The plaintiff brings a civil lawsuit; the defendant is the party being sued.
A suspect is someone police consider possibly guilty before charges; a defendant has been formally charged or sued in court.

collocations: the defendant in a civil suit

examples.everyday: My neighbor is the defendant in a small claims case over a fence, and he is really stressed about it.
examples.professional: Our legal team asked the court to dismiss the claim because the defendant company never had a contract with the plaintiff.
examples.analytical: In adversarial systems, the defendant's presumption of innocence shifts the burden of proof onto the state.

nuance.analogy: In a courtroom game, the defendant is the one who must answer the challenge, like the team that has to respond to the other side's move.
nuance.etymology: From Old French defendant, from Latin defendere 'to ward off, defend'.
common_mistakes: Using defendant for a witness or a victim.
Saying 'the defendent' with an extra e; the spelling is defendant.

defendant.etymology: From Middle English *defendaunt* (“defending; defending in a suit”), borrowed from Old French *defendant*, present participle of *defendre*, from Latin *dēfendō*.

senses.definition: Great pleasure; delight.

core.definition: Great pleasure or delight, especially in something enjoyed slowly and fully.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, TAY, and reduce the -tion ending to 'shun'. Avoid turning the middle syllables into full vowels.

nuance.connotation: Positive, with an old-fashioned, elegant tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use delectation in speech. It appears in older literature, some religious writing, and essays about pleasure. In everyday talk people say delight or enjoyment. If you read it in a text, treat it as a more formal synonym for pleasure.

distinctions.note: Delight is common and everyday, while delectation is rare and literary.
Pleasure is the everyday word, while delectation often suggests a richer, more absorbing enjoyment.

examples.everyday: The kids watched the fireworks with obvious delectation.
examples.professional: The workshop was a source of delectation for the team, who left it energized.
examples.analytical: The writer treats the sensory delectation of the garden as a foretaste of spiritual joy.

nuance.analogy: Delectation is like a slow sip of very old wine: the pleasure lingers and is savored.
nuance.etymology: From Latin delectatio, from delectare (to delight).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as del-ek-TAY-shun with a flat final syllable.
Using delectation in casual talk where delight is more natural.

delectation.etymology: Attested from the mid 14th century, from Old French *delectation* (“enjoyment”), from Latin *dēlectātiōnem*, accusative singular of *dēlectātiō*, from the verb Latin *dēlectō* (“to delight, charm, please”), frequentative of *dēliciō*, from *de-* (“away”) +…

senses.definition: Insane; mentally ill.
Having dementia.
Crazy; ridiculous.
senses.example: a demented idea

core.definition: Mentally confused or disturbed, often used for someone with dementia; informally, crazy or ridiculous.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MEN, the second syllable. The final syllable is a reduced 'id', not 'eed', so it rhymes with 'rented'.

nuance.connotation: Negative and sometimes harsh. In medical contexts it is an older term, while in casual speech it can be an insult or a strong exaggeration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'demented' in its medical sense sparingly, since 'dementia' and 'cognitive decline' are preferred in health care. In casual speech 'demented' means crazy or ridiculous, as in 'a demented idea.' Using it about a person with memory loss can sound cruel, so it is best avoided in that situation.

distinctions.note: Crazy is very common and casual, and can be affectionate; demented is stronger and more clinical or harsh.
Confused describes a temporary state of not understanding; demented suggests a deeper, longer mental disturbance.
Insane is an older, legal or strong term for severe mental illness; demented is more about dementia or wild, irrational ideas.

examples.everyday: That traffic jam at rush hour is demented, so let's take the back roads instead.
examples.professional: The vendor's pricing model looks demented, so we should check the assumptions before we sign anything.
examples.analytical: Swift's satire depicts the projectors of Laputa as demented, showing how abstraction can detach thinkers from ordinary reality.

nuance.analogy: Calling an idea demented is like saying the map has gone so wrong that it leads you off a cliff.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dēmēns, 'out of one's mind', from dē- 'away from' and mēns 'mind'.
common_mistakes: Using 'demented' for a person with memory loss in a polite conversation, where 'dementia' or 'memory problems' is kinder.
Confusing it with 'dementia', which is the noun for the condition.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'eed'.

senses.definition: The act of naming or designating.
That by which anything is denominated or styled; an epithet; a name, designation, or title; especially, a general name indicating a class of like individuals.
A class, or society of individuals, called by the same name; a subdivision of a religion.
senses.example: She follows the Ahmadiyya denomination of Islam.

senses.definition: A unit in a series of units of weight, money, etc.
senses.example: What denomination is that money? They are all 50 euro notes.

core.definition: A large organized branch of a religion, especially of Christianity, with its own name, beliefs and leadership, such as Baptist or Methodist.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on NAY, with secondary stress on 'nom'. Many Americans say the second syllable with /ɑ/ because of the cot-caught merger, so 'nah' is natural. Reduce the vowels in 'dih' and 'muh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the word describes a group without judging it. In some evangelical circles, 'denominational' can imply institutional rigidity.
nuance.usage_note: In the US, 'denomination' is the standard word for a Christian church family. Americans ask 'What denomination are you?' fairly casually, but it can feel personal. It is also used for money, as in bills of different denominations.

distinctions.note: Sect often implies a smaller, more separate or sometimes extreme group, while denomination is a neutral term for an established body.
Church can mean a congregation, a building or the whole Christian body, while denomination names a family of churches.
Faith or religion refers to the broad tradition, such as Christianity, while denomination is a subdivision within it.
Cult is pejorative and suggests control and extreme devotion, while denomination is neutral.

examples.everyday: I grew up in a small-town church, but I'm not sure what denomination it was.
examples.professional: The study surveyed members of every major denomination to compare views on volunteering.
examples.analytical: The proliferation of denominations in American Protestantism reflects both the freedom of religious association and persistent disputes over doctrine and polity.

nuance.analogy: Like branches of one tree, each with its own shape but a common trunk.
nuance.etymology: From Latin denominare, 'to name', from de- + nomen, 'name'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable; it is NAY, not NOM.
Saying 'denomination' for a single congregation; that is a church or parish.
Using 'sect' as a neutral synonym; it can sound negative.

traditions.view: Orthodox Christians generally do not call the Orthodox Church a denomination; they see it as the one Church in continuity with the apostles and view Protestant groupings as divisions outside it.

Catholics teach that the Church of Christ subsists in the Catholic Church, and they usually do not call it a denomination; they recognize elements of truth and sanctification in other Christian communities.

Many Protestants accept the concept of denominations, seeing the visible church as legitimately diverse, while holding that all true believers form one invisible church. Some nondenominational and Baptist groups prefer to emphasize congregational independence.

denomination.etymology: From Middle English *denominacioun*, from Old French *denominacion*, from Latin *dēnōminātiō*.

senses.definition: To reduce the level of priority of.
senses.example: Do you want me to deprioritize my current report to get this done?

core.definition: To lower the importance or urgency of a task, project, or item so that it is handled later.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on OR, and the first syllable has a lighter secondary stress. Say the stressed syllable clearly and keep the -ize ending as the sound /aɪz/, like tize.

nuance.connotation: neutral, a workplace term that can sound slightly negative to the person affected
nuance.usage_note: Deprioritize is common in American offices, especially in meetings, Slack messages, and project planning. Teams say we are going to deprioritize X when they decide to delay it. It can sound like a polite way to say that something is being dropped, so people often add until next quarter or for now. A common reply is Got it, or Makes sense.

distinctions.note: Postpone means to move an event or task to a later time, while deprioritize means to rank it lower in importance, often without a fixed new date.
Delay implies a stopping or slowing caused by a problem, while deprioritize describes a deliberate decision about importance.

examples.everyday: I'm going to deprioritize cleaning the garage this weekend and just do the dishes.
examples.professional: Given the launch deadline, we're going to deprioritize the dashboard redesign until next quarter.
examples.analytical: When budget pressure rose, the committee deprioritized long-term equity goals in favor of immediate cost savings.

nuance.analogy: Like moving a file from the top of your desk to a drawer, deprioritize keeps the task but takes it out of your immediate focus.
nuance.etymology: Formed from de- plus prioritize, from priority, from Medieval Latin prioritas 'being earlier', from prior 'earlier'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in dee-pry-or-IH-tize, when the main stress is on OR.
Using deprioritize with a person as object, when it is normally used for tasks, projects, or items.

conversation.text: We decided to deprioritize the mobile app until next year.
If we add this feature, what should we deprioritize?
The redesign got deprioritized after the budget cuts.

senses.definition: Of or concerning the devil: devilish, satanic.
Extremely wicked or cruel.
senses.example: a diabolical plan

senses.definition: (Devilishly) cunning or devious.
Crazy, wild (sometimes especially due to being unexpected or surprising).

core.definition: Extremely cruel, wicked or evil; also, informally, very unpleasant or difficult, as in 'diabolical traffic'.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BAH, the third syllable. The final syllables are quick and reduced, so say 'kul' rather than a full 'i-cal'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. In everyday speech it can be used hyperbolically for something annoying, which is milder but still negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use diabolical for serious wickedness in news, fiction and political speech, and for a clever, cruel plan. In casual talk, people use it humorously for something terrible, like a diabolical parking meter. Calling someone diabolical is strong, so use it only when you mean it or want a dramatic effect.

distinctions.note: Devilish can be mild or playful, as in a devilish grin, while diabolical is stronger and implies real cruelty or evil.
Satanic refers specifically to Satan or his worship, while diabolical describes wicked or cunning behavior in general.

examples.everyday: Sitting in this traffic is diabolical; I've been stuck on the freeway for an hour.
examples.professional: The vendor's billing system is diabolical, and it cost us two weeks of reconciliation work.
examples.analytical: Milton's Satan is diabolical not merely in his deeds but in his eloquent self-justification.

nuance.analogy: Like a villain's scheme so elaborate and cruel that it seems designed by the devil himself.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin diabolicus, from Greek diabolos 'slanderer, accuser', from diaballein 'to throw across'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'dy-uh-BOLE-ih-kul'; the stress is on BAH.
Using it for mild misbehavior; for a kid who is simply naughty, 'mischievous' is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Septuagint and the New Testament, diabolos (accuser, slanderer) is the usual Greek term for the devil, the adversary of God and humanity. Key passages: Matthew 4:1 describes Jesus being tempted by the devil in the wilderness. Revelation 12:9 identifies the great dragon as the ancient serpent called the Devil and Satan. John 8:44 has Jesus describe the devil as a liar and a murderer from the beginning.

senses.definition: Causing disruption or unrest.
senses.example: Children who exhibit disruptive behavior may be expelled from school.

senses.definition: Causing major change, as in a market.
senses.example: disruptive technologies

core.definition: Causing disorder or interrupting normal activity, or, in business, bringing major change that displaces existing ways of doing things.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on RUHP. Keep the middle syllable reduced, so it sounds like dis-RUHP-tiv rather than dis-ruh-PTIV.

nuance.connotation: Negative in a classroom or meeting, but positive in business, where disruptive innovation is praised.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday speech, Americans call a child or a noisy guest disruptive when they cause trouble in a group. In business and technology, disruptive is a favorite word for products or companies that change a market, and it is usually praised. Context decides whether it is criticism or compliment.

distinctions.note: Disturbing describes something that upsets or troubles you emotionally; disruptive describes something that interferes with activity.
Innovative means new or creative; disruptive specifically means the new thing overturns the old market or practice.

examples.everyday: The kids got pretty disruptive at the back of the restaurant, so we asked for the check.
examples.professional: Remote work was a disruptive change for our team, but it also made our hiring much more flexible.
examples.analytical: The reform proved disruptive not merely to the old institutions but to the assumptions that had justified them.

nuance.analogy: Like a pebble dropped in a calm pond, sending ripples across the whole surface.
nuance.etymology: From Latin disrumpere, 'to break apart', via disruptus.
common_mistakes: Confusing disruptive with disturbed, which describes a person's emotional state.
Stressing the second syllable, saying dis-RUP-tiv with a short u instead of a long uh.

core.definition: In the Bible, an Edomite servant of King Saul who reported David's visit to the priests at Nob and later killed them.
