common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'c' as 'k', as in 'JAK-inth'.
Assuming jacinth is a common everyday word rather than an old or literary term.
nuance.biblical_note: In the RSV, jacinth translates the Greek word hyakinthos, a precious stone. It appears in Revelation 21:20, where it is one of the twelve stones forming the foundations of the New Jerusalem. Its use there suggests the beauty and splendor of the city.

jacinth.etymology: From Middle English *jacynct*, partly from Old French *jacincte*, and partly from Old English *iacinþ*, both from Medieval Latin *jacintus*, *jacinthus*, from Latin *hyacinthus*, from Ancient Greek *ὑάκινθος*.

senses.definition: Airy; showy; finical.
Characterized by an affected or fantastical manner.
Dapper or stylish.
senses.example: He wore a jaunty outfit that was all the rage.

senses.definition: Ostentatiously self-confident.
senses.example: He walked down the street with a jaunty swaggering step, as if daring others less perfectly satisfied to intrude upon his good mood.

senses.definition: A master-at-arms on board a Royal Navy ship.

core.definition: Cheerfully confident and lively; having a bright, stylish or carefree manner or appearance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a light ee. Keep the first vowel short and open, like the vowel in caught.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests a cheerful, confident, sometimes slightly showy mood or style.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use jaunty to describe a person who walks, dresses or talks with bright confidence, as in a jaunty hat or a jaunty tune. It is a compliment in most contexts. The noun sense, a master-at-arms on a Royal Navy ship, is mainly British and rarely used in American English.

distinctions.note: Cheerful describes a general happy mood, while jaunty adds a sense of brisk, stylish self-assurance in appearance or movement.
Flashy means showy and attention-seeking, often in a negative way; jaunty is more lighthearted and can be charming.

examples.everyday: He wore a jaunty red scarf and whistled as he walked into the coffee shop.
examples.professional: The jaunty tone of the slide deck made the serious budget news easier to hear.
examples.analytical: The narrator's jaunty voice works as an ironic mask that hides the story's darker logic.

nuance.analogy: A jaunty person is like a song in a major key with a quick, bouncy beat.
nuance.etymology: Probably from French gentil, genteel, through an earlier sense of smart or fashionable.
common_mistakes: Using jaunty for a serious or dignified manner; it suggests lightness.
Pronouncing the first vowel as a long ay sound, as in JAYN-tee.

core.definition: In the Bible, the fourth son of Japheth and grandson of Noah, ancestor of the Ionian Greeks and their lands.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make the second syllable a reduced schwa. Avoid giving it three full syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a name and a historical or genealogical term in biblical study.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet Javan in Bible study, church reading or history courses on the ancient Near East. Scholars often identify it with the Ionians or with Greece generally. It is rarely used outside religious and academic contexts.

distinctions.note: A different biblical figure, Javan's name is sometimes confused with Jabal, Jubal or Jabin in other passages.

examples.everyday: In our Bible study, someone asked who Javan was, and we looked up Genesis 10.
examples.professional: The sermon series on the table of nations explained Javan as the ancestor of the Greek peoples.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether Javan in Genesis 10 refers to Ionia specifically or to the Greek world more broadly.

nuance.analogy: Javan is like a family tree's early branch: a name in the genealogy that stands for a whole people who later grew famous.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Yāwān, the name for the Ionian Greeks.
common_mistakes: Confusing Javan with Jabal or Jubal, other names in Genesis.
Saying JAH-van instead of JAY-vun.
nuance.biblical_note: Javan is the Hebrew Yāwān (יָוָן), a name for the Ionian Greeks and the Greek world. In Genesis 10:2 and 10:4 (RSV) he is named as a son of Japheth and the grandfather of Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim and Dodanim. Ezekiel 27:13 (RSV) lists Javan among traders who dealt with Tire, and Isaiah 66:19 (RSV) mentions Javan among distant nations.

core.definition: An English form of the name Jeremiah, the name of the Old Testament prophet; in the Bible itself the name appears only as Jeremiah.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The 'r' is pronounced clearly, and the final vowel is a light 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Jeremy is a very common given name in the United States. When you talk about the Bible, say Jeremiah for the prophet, since that is the form used in standard English translations such as the RSV. Americans may use Jeremy casually for anyone with that name.
word_family: Jeremiad (noun, a prolonged lament or complaint)

distinctions.note: Jeremy is the familiar English form used for people today; Jeremiah is the spelling used for the Hebrew prophet in Bible translations.

examples.everyday: Jeremy is bringing the chips to the barbecue on Saturday.
examples.professional: Jeremy will own the data pipeline migration, so please send him your questions by Thursday.
examples.analytical: The name Jeremy descends from Jeremiah, which means that the modern form still carries the Hebrew name of the prophet.

nuance.analogy: Like a nickname that grew into its own name: the same root, a more familiar shape.
nuance.etymology: English form of Latin Jeremias, from Greek Ieremias, from Hebrew Yirmeyahu.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'JER-ee-my' with three equal syllables; the middle syllable is weak.
Using Jeremy when quoting the prophet in a Bible passage; the RSV uses Jeremiah.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible itself the name appears as Jeremiah, the prophet of Judah active around 627 to 586 BC. The English Jeremy derives from Hebrew Yirmeyahu, and in the New Testament Matthew 16:14 and Matthew 2:17 refer to Jeremiah. The name is the same person, not a different one.

core.definition: In the Bible, the priest of Midian and father-in-law of Moses, who advised Moses to appoint judges to share the work of leading Israel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The "th" is voiceless, as in "thin", and the final vowel is a long "oh" sound.

nuance.connotation: neutral; it is a biblical name and does not carry a special emotional tone outside religious settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often meet Jethro in Bible study, Sunday school, or discussions of Moses. It also appears in the popular TV comedy character name, so some people may think of that. In a religious conversation, you can say "Jethro, Moses' father-in-law" to clarify who he is.

distinctions.note: Jether is Gideon's son; Jethro is Moses' father-in-law. They are different people with similar names.
Reuel is another name used for Moses' father-in-law in Exodus 2:18; in the RSV, the name Jethro is used in Exodus 3 and 18.

examples.everyday: My friend says her grandfather is like Jethro in the Bible, always giving practical advice.
examples.professional: When we design the approval process, we borrow the idea from Jethro's advice to Moses about sharing the load.
examples.analytical: Jethro's counsel in Exodus 18 presents delegation as a wise form of leadership rather than a sign of weakness.

nuance.analogy: Jethro is like a wise mentor who sees a leader working too hard and suggests a better system.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Yitro (יִתְרוֹ), perhaps meaning "his excellence" or "abundance".
common_mistakes: Using "Jethro" as the name of Moses' brother; the Bible names Aaron as Moses' brother.
Mispronouncing the "th" as a "t" or "d" sound.
nuance.biblical_note: Jethro, Hebrew Yitro, is a priest of Midian and father-in-law of Moses, whose daughter Zipporah marries Moses. Exodus 3:1 identifies him as the priest of Midian who was Moses' father-in-law, and Exodus 18 describes his visit to Moses in the wilderness. In Exodus 18, Jethro sees Moses judging the people all day and advises him to appoint capable judges to share the work.

core.definition: An ancient port city on the Mediterranean coast of Canaan, today part of Jaffa in Tel Aviv, Israel, where ships from Phoenicia and beyond landed cargo.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the final vowel short and soft, like the end of 'Tokyo' without the y sound. Americans often say it the same way as the Jaffa in modern Israel, so you can use either name.

nuance.connotation: neutral; a place name with no positive or negative charge, though its Bible stories often involve God's call to unexpected people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mainly meet Joppa in Bible reading, church teaching, or history discussions. In everyday talk, most people say Jaffa for the modern city. Joppa is a neutral, biblical place name and can be used in a sermon or Bible study without any awkwardness.

distinctions.note: Joppa is the biblical and historical name, while Jaffa is the modern Arabic-derived name for the same place, now part of Tel Aviv.
Caesarea was a later port built by Herod the Great further up the coast, while Joppa was the older harbor used by Solomon and mentioned throughout Scripture.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group is reading about Peter staying in Joppa, so we looked up where it is on a map.
examples.professional: In the seminar slides, the map marks Joppa as the main Mediterranean harbor for building the Temple.
examples.analytical: Luke's narrative places Peter's vision and his stay in Joppa at a hinge point, where the gospel moves beyond Jewish boundaries toward the Gentiles.

nuance.analogy: Joppa is like a seaport that connects a country to the wider world, the place where the Bible's story first crosses the water.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Yafo, meaning 'beautiful' or 'beauty'.
common_mistakes: Saying the ending like 'poppa' with a long a instead of a short schwa.
Using Joppa for the modern city without noting that Americans usually say Jaffa today.
nuance.biblical_note: Joppa was the harbor through which cedar timber from Lebanon reached Jerusalem for Solomon's Temple (2 Chronicles 2:16). Jonah sailed from Joppa to flee from God's call to preach to Nineveh (Jonah 1:3). In Acts, Peter raised Tabitha, also called Dorcas, to life there (Acts 9:36-43) and received the vision of the sheet that led him to visit Cornelius (Acts 10:9-16).

senses.definition: Having lots of juice.
senses.example: a juicy peach

senses.definition: Exciting; titillating.
senses.example: I do not keep up with all the latest juicy rumors.

senses.definition: Voluptuous, curvy, thick; sexy in those ways.
Muscular due to steroid use.
Strong; thus, also painful.

core.definition: Full of juice or liquid, or, informally, exciting, scandalous or tempting, especially in gossip or a story.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, JOO. The final 'y' sounds like a long 'ee'. Do not say 'JOO-zee' with a z sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive for food, and playful or mildly negative for gossip. The sexual sense is informal and can be rude in mixed company.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'juicy' for fruit, meat and steak, like 'a juicy burger.' For gossip, they say 'juicy details' or 'juicy story,' which is casual and fun. The sense of voluptuous or sexy is informal and can sound inappropriate at work or with acquaintances.

distinctions.note: 'Moist' suggests slight dampness and is often neutral or slightly negative for food; 'juicy' suggests liquid that is pleasant and flavorful.
'Tender' describes texture, meaning easy to chew; 'juicy' describes the liquid that a food releases.

examples.everyday: That burger was so juicy I had to grab a napkin right away.
examples.professional: The juicy details of the vendor's contract issue came out in the meeting, so legal is now involved.
examples.analytical: The novel relies on juicy scandal to attract readers, yet its moral argument is more subtle than the gossip suggests.

nuance.analogy: Like a ripe orange that bursts when you bite it: full of liquid and flavor.
nuance.etymology: From juice (Old French jus) plus the adjective suffix -y, 'full of juice.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as 'zee' with a voiced s, as in 'JOO-zee.'
Using the sexual sense in polite or work situations.
Confusing 'juicy' with 'juice' as an adjective; 'juicy' is the adjective.

conversation.text: This peach is so juicy that it's dripping down my arm.
The burger was thick and juicy.
Tell me all the juicy details!

senses.definition: Government under the control of a nation's worst or least-qualified citizens.

core.definition: Government run by a nation's worst or least-qualified citizens, usually a term of criticism for corrupt or incompetent leadership.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the third syllable, TAH, and the final -cy is a reduced 'see.' Learners often stress the first syllable or pronounce the middle -cra- as a full syllable; the American r in 'kruh' is flapped lightly.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It is an insult aimed at a government, implying that its leaders are the worst possible choice.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in political commentary, editorials, and opinion writing, often to criticize an administration. It is not used for ordinary workplaces or casual talk. It sounds deliberately sharp, so use it with care when discussing real officials.

distinctions.note: An oligarchy is rule by a small elite, which is a structural description; kakistocracy describes the quality of the rulers as the worst available.
A plutocracy is rule by the wealthy; kakistocracy says nothing about wealth and only judges leaders as unfit or corrupt.

examples.everyday: My uncle thinks the city council is a kakistocracy, and he complains about it every time we eat dinner together.
examples.professional: In the policy memo, the author argued that a hiring freeze combined with political appointments would turn the agency into a kakistocracy.
examples.analytical: Plato's worry about rule by unqualified men anticipates the modern charge that democratic systems can slide into kakistocracy when merit is replaced by loyalty.

nuance.analogy: If a sports team were run by its least skilled players, the team would be a kakistocracy, the reverse of a meritocracy.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kakistos, 'worst,' and -kratia, 'rule.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (KAK-ih-stock-ra-see) instead of the third syllable, -TAH-.
Confusing it with 'aristocracy,' which means rule by the best or by a hereditary upper class.

kakistocracy.etymology: From Ancient Greek *κάκιστος* (“worst”), superlative of *κακός* (“bad”) + *-κρατία* (“power, rule, government”) (corresponding to *-cracy*).

senses.definition: The traversal of one length of the pool, or (less commonly) one length and back again.
senses.example: to swim two laps

senses.definition: The part of the clothing that lies on the knees or thighs when one sits down; that part of the person thus covered.
The loose part of a coat; the lower part of a garment that plays loosely; a skirt; an apron.
An edge; a border; a hem, as of cloth.
A place of rearing and fostering.
The upper legs of a seated person.
senses.example: The boy was sitting on his mother's lap.

senses.definition: A component that overlaps or covers any portion of itself or of an adjacent component.
The act or process of lapping.
That part of any substance or fixture which extends over, or lies upon, or by the side of, a part of another.
senses.example: the lap of a board

senses.definition: The state or condition of being in part extended over or by the side of something else; or the extent of the overlapping.
senses.example: The second boat got a lap of half its length on the leader.

senses.definition: The amount by which a slide valve at its half stroke overlaps a port in the seat, being equal to the distance the valve must move from its mid stroke position in order to begin to open the port. Used alone, lap refers to outside lap (see below).
In card playing and other games, the points won in excess of the number necessary to complete a game;—so called when they are counted in the score of the following game.
A sheet, layer, or bat, of cotton fiber prepared for the carding machine.

A piece of brass, lead, or other soft metal, used to hold a cutting or polishing powder in cutting glass, gems, etc. or in polishing cutlery or in toolmaking. It is usually in the form of a wheel or disk that revolves on a vertical axis.
The taking of liquid into the mouth with the tongue.
Clipping of laparoscopy.
Clipping of laparotomy.
One circuit around a race track.
senses.example: to run twenty laps

senses.definition: To enfold; to hold as in one's lap; to cherish.
To rest or recline in someone's lap, or as in a lap.
To fold; to bend and lay over or on something.
senses.example: to lap a piece of cloth

senses.definition: To wrap around, enwrap, wrap up.
senses.example: to lap a bandage around a finger

senses.definition: To envelop, enfold.
senses.example: lapped in luxury

senses.definition: To wind around.
To place or lay (one thing) so as to overlap another.
senses.example: One laps roof tiles so that water can run off.

senses.definition: To polish (a surface, especially metal or gemstone) with very fine abrasive to achieve smoothness and small dimensional changes.
To be turned or folded; to lie partly on or over something; to overlap.
senses.example: The cloth laps back.

senses.definition: To cut or polish with a lap, as glass, gems, cutlery, etc.
To take (liquid) into the mouth with the tongue; to lick up with a quick motion of the tongue.
senses.example: Don’t lap your soup like that! You look like a dog.

senses.definition: To wash against a surface with a splashing sound; to swash.
To overtake a straggler in a race by completing one more whole lap than the straggler.
Clipping of laparoscopic.

core.definition: The top of the thighs when you sit down, where a child or pet can sit; the area across a seated person's legs.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short, relaxed vowel like the a in cat, not the ah of father. The final p is released without a puff of air.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses; warm and comforting when a child or pet sits on your lap.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lap for the body part constantly in everyday speech, as in 'Come sit on my lap.' For a swimming lap, Americans say lap too, but for the coat part they often say the lapel for the folded front of a jacket. The lap of a skirt or coat is less common in speech.

distinctions.note: The knee is a joint; the lap is the broader area across the thighs and knees when seated.
The thigh is one part of the leg, while lap refers to the whole seated surface formed by both thighs.

examples.everyday: Come sit on Grandpa's lap and tell me about your day.
examples.professional: I balanced my laptop on my lap during the call because the desk was full.
examples.analytical: The phrase 'in the lap of the gods' turns a seated body into an image of fate, which shows how bodily words carry moral meaning.

nuance.analogy: Your lap is like a little shelf that your thighs make when you sit down.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English lappe, meaning a fold or flap of cloth.
common_mistakes: Saying 'lahp' with a long vowel; the American vowel is short.
Confusing lap (body part) with lamp or lab in fast speech.

lap.etymology: From Middle English *lappe*, from Old English *læppa* (“skirt or flap of a garment”), from **lappō*, from Proto-Germanic **lappô* (“cloth; rag”), of origin, possibly Proto-Indo-European **leb-* (“to hang loosely”).

conversation.text: I try to swim twenty laps every morning.
Is the pool open for lap swimming right now?
The dog fell asleep in my lap during the drive.

senses.definition: Not governed by any law.
Prohibited by law; unlawful, illegal.
Not restrained by the law or by discipline; disorderly, unruly.
senses.example: On why leaving lawless places and leaving pseudovirtuous groups is loving such places and groups

core.definition: Without respect for laws or rules; behaving in a wild, disorderly, or criminal way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a weak uh sound, not a long ee, so it rhymes with the second part of 'careless'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies disorder, danger, or defiance of authority.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lawless for places or times without effective police or government, such as a lawless frontier or a lawless area after a disaster. In everyday talk it is strong, so avoid using it for a minor rule-breaker. Describing a person as lawless suggests a serious character issue.

distinctions.note: Illegal means against the law in a specific way, while lawless describes a general absence of order or respect for law.
Unruly describes behavior that is hard to control, usually in a less serious way than lawless.

examples.everyday: After the storm, some neighborhoods felt lawless, so people stayed indoors until the police came back.
examples.professional: The vendor operated in a lawless market with no reliable contracts, so we moved our servers to a regulated region.
examples.analytical: Hobbes argues that without a sovereign power, human life would be solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and lawless.

nuance.analogy: A lawless place is like a playground with no referee: everyone plays by their own rules until someone gets hurt.
nuance.etymology: From law, plus the suffix -less meaning without.
common_mistakes: Confusing lawless with lawful, which has the opposite meaning.
Using lawless for a minor offense; it is a strong word for serious disorder.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word anomos, meaning without law or lawless, appears in 2 Thessalonians 2:8 for a figure who opposes God. In 1 Timothy 1:9 Paul says the law is laid down for the lawless and disobedient, meaning people who ignore God's commands. The word describes a person who sets aside divine law.

senses.definition: Given to excessive sexual activity and debauchery.

core.definition: Showing an excessive, often predatory, interest in sex and sexual pleasure, usually in a way that others find offensive.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LECH, and the middle syllable is a reduced schwa-r. Say it as three syllables, 'LECH-er-us,' not 'lee-cher-us.'

nuance.connotation: negative. It is a strong moral judgment and should be used carefully.
nuance.usage_note: Lecherous is a strong, negative word used in formal writing or to describe someone who harasses others. It is not casual; in conversation Americans more often say 'creepy' or 'sleazy.' Because it is a serious accusation, use it only with clear evidence or in literary description.

distinctions.note: Lascivious is more literary and emphasizes lustful desire, often in art or description, while lecherous describes a person's conduct.
Creepy is an informal word for unsettling behavior and is much milder than lecherous.
Lewd describes crude or obscene language or behavior, while lecherous describes a person driven by sexual appetite.

examples.everyday: My friend said the man at the party gave her a lecherous stare, so she left early.
examples.professional: HR reviewed complaints that a manager made lecherous comments, which violates our conduct policy.
examples.analytical: The novel portrays the landlord as lecherous, using his desire as a sign of a broader moral decay in the town.

nuance.analogy: Like a fox circling a henhouse, watching for any opening.
nuance.etymology: From Old French lechier, 'to lick, to live in debauchery,' probably from a Germanic source.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'lee,' when it is short, as in 'LECH.'
Using 'lecherous' for mild flirting; it is a strong moral accusation.

lecherous.etymology: From Middle English *lecherous*, *licherous*, from Old French **lecherous*, from Old French *lecherie*, *licherie* (“gluttony, sensuality, lewdness, lechery”), from Old French *lecher*, *lechier*, *lekier*, *lescher* (“to lick, live in gluttony or…

senses.definition: To raise or rise.
senses.example: The fog eventually lifted, leaving the streets clear.

senses.definition: To cause to move upwards.
To steal.
To source directly without acknowledgement; to plagiarize.
To arrest (a person).
To remove (a ban, restriction, etc.).
To alleviate, to lighten (pressure, tension, stress, etc.)
To lift weights; to weight-lift.
senses.example: She lifts twice a week at the gym.

senses.definition: To try to raise something; to exert the strength for raising or bearing.
To elevate or improve in rank, condition, etc. often with up.
To collect, as moneys due; to raise.
Given morphisms f and g with the same target: To produce a morphism which the given morphism factors through (i.e. a morphism h such that f=g∘h; cf. lift n.etymology 1, noun 20)
To transform (a function) into a corresponding function in a different context.
To buy a security or other asset previously offered for sale.
To take (hounds) off the existing scent and move them to another spot.
An act of lifting or raising.
The act of transporting someone in a vehicle; a ride; a trip.
senses.example: He gave me a lift to the bus station.

senses.definition: A mechanical device for raising vehicles for service, so that it is easier for a mechanic to get beneath them.
An upward force; especially, the force (generated by wings, rotary wings, or airfoils) that keeps aircraft aloft.
Any technique for lifting weights.
The difference in elevation between the upper pool and lower pool of a waterway, separated by lock.
The lifting of a dance partner into the air.
Permanent construction with a built-in platform that is lifted vertically.
An improvement in mood.
The amount or weight to be lifted.
senses.example: What's the maximum lift of this crane?

senses.definition: The space or distance through which anything is lifted.
A rise; a degree of elevation.
senses.example: the lift of a lock in canals

senses.definition: A liftgate.
One of the steps of a cone pulley.
A layer of leather in the heel of a shoe.
That portion of the vibration of a balance during which the impulse is given.
A morphism which some given morphism factors through; i.e. given a pair of morphisms f:X→Y and g:Z→Y, a morphism h such that f=g∘h. (In this case h is said to be a lift of f via Z or via g).
A shorter extract from a commercial/advertisement, able to be used on its own.
A rope leading from the masthead to the extremity of a yard below, and used for raising or supporting the end of the yard.
A thief.

core.definition: To raise something to a higher position, or to move it upward.

pronunciation.tip: This is a one-syllable word with a short i, like the i in sit. Do not lengthen it to a long ee sound, and keep the f and t clear at the end.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It is a basic physical action word with no strong emotional tone, though lift can also mean to improve someone's mood.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lift in everyday speech for moving heavy objects, offering a ride, or boosting spirits. For a ride, Americans say give someone a ride or give someone a lift, and both are natural. In shops, an elevator is the usual word for a lift, which is mainly British.

distinctions.note: Raise is more general and can apply to abstract things, such as raising prices; lift suggests moving something physically upward.
Carry means to hold something and move it from one place to another, while lift focuses on moving it upward.

examples.everyday: Can you give me a hand and lift this box onto the shelf?
examples.professional: The team will lift the restrictions on the dashboard once the data pipeline passes review.
examples.analytical: Her argument is that criticism should lift the reader's understanding rather than merely expose errors.

nuance.analogy: Like a crane lifting a load, lift means raising something from a lower place to a higher one.
nuance.etymology: From Old Norse lypta, meaning to raise up in the air.
common_mistakes: Using lift for the American elevator; say elevator in the US.
Saying lift me up as a request for a ride; say give me a ride instead.

senses.definition: To detest, hate, or revile (someone or something).
senses.example: I loathe scrubbing toilets.

core.definition: To feel intense hatred or disgust for someone or something; to detest or revile.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the single syllable, with a voiced 'th' at the end, like the 'th' in 'breathe'. Many learners devoice it to sound like 'loath'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. 'Loathe' expresses deep hatred, so use it carefully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I loathe' for strong dislike of things like traffic, cold calls or cilantro, often with humor. Saying it about a person is much stronger and can sound harsh. The gerund is common: 'I loathe waiting in line.' A natural reply to someone's complaint might be 'Tell me about it.'

distinctions.note: 'Hate' is the everyday word and is less intense in casual speech. 'Loathe' sounds more emphatic and deliberate.
'Detest' is a bit more formal and cool in tone. 'Loathe' sounds more emotional.
'Despise' implies contempt or looking down on someone. 'Loathe' implies disgust.

collocations: loathe being told what to do

examples.everyday: I loathe grocery shopping on Saturdays, so I always go on Tuesday.
examples.professional: Our team loathes meetings that run past their scheduled time, so we always send an agenda.
examples.analytical: Kant could not simply loathe the moral failures he described; he sought their rational root.

nuance.analogy: Loathe is like a strong, cold wind that pushes you away from something, rather than a light breeze.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'lāthian', meaning to be hostile to, related to 'loath'.
common_mistakes: Using 'loathe' for mild dislike, which sounds dramatic in American conversation.
Saying 'loathe to' instead of 'loathe doing', as in 'I loathe to wait' (incorrect in most contexts).

loathe.etymology: From Middle English *lothe*, from Old English *lāþian*, from **laiþēn*, from Proto-Germanic **laiþāną*.

senses.definition: A low-level interdependent coupling between program modules.
The situation where ties between people and groups in an organization are not as strong as those recognized by theories of bureaucracy.

core.definition: A software design principle in which modules depend on each other as little as possible, so that changing one module does not break the others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on both words, with LOOS and KUP-ling as the main stresses. The oo in loose is the long 'oo' as in 'goose', and the -ing ends in a soft ng.

nuance.connotation: Positive in software design, where it describes a desirable, flexible architecture.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'loose coupling' in software engineering, system design, and architecture discussions. It is technical, so use it with engineers rather than in casual talk. In organizational studies it can describe weak ties between departments, so say which sense you mean in a mixed group.

distinctions.note: 'Tight coupling' means modules depend closely on each other, which makes changes harder and riskier.
'Cohesion' describes how well the parts of one module work together, while 'coupling' describes how modules depend on each other.

examples.everyday: My friend who works in software says that good apps have loose coupling so one part can change without breaking the rest.
examples.professional: We moved the payment service behind an event queue to achieve loose coupling, so the checkout team can deploy independently.
examples.analytical: Loose coupling reduces the number of assumptions one module must make about another, which makes a system easier to reason about and to change.

nuance.analogy: Like a set of power outlets on a wall, loose coupling lets you plug in and unplug devices without rewiring the house.
nuance.etymology: Coupling comes from the Latin copulare, meaning to join together.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'loose coupling' with 'loosely coupled' as a noun versus an adjective.
Pronouncing 'coupling' with a long u sound, as in 'cupling'.

senses.definition: A feeling of strong desire, especially such a feeling driven by sexual arousal.
senses.example: Seeing Leslie fills me with a passionate lust.

senses.definition: Virility; vigor; active power.
To look at or watch with a strong desire, especially of a sexual nature.

core.definition: A strong desire, especially a sexual desire, or an intense craving for something.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short u vowel as in 'cup' and end with a clear st cluster. Do not add a vowel between s and t.

nuance.connotation: negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lust for sexual desire, but also for a strong craving, as in 'a lust for power.' In everyday talk, the word can sound harsh or judgmental, so people often say 'attraction' or 'desire' instead. In religious contexts, lust usually has a moral meaning.

distinctions.note: Desire is a neutral or positive word for wanting something, while lust is stronger and often carries a moral or sexual sense.
Greed is an excessive wish for money or possessions, while lust may be sexual or a strong craving for power or pleasure.

examples.everyday: The ads play on people's lust for quick results, but I try not to fall for them.
examples.professional: The report warns that a lust for growth can push the team to ignore quality.
examples.analytical: Jesus treats lust as an inward act of the heart, not merely a physical deed.

nuance.analogy: Lust is like a fire that burns hottest when it is fed without limit.
nuance.etymology: From Old English lust, pleasure or desire.
common_mistakes: Using lust as a neutral word for liking something; it is much stronger.
Saying 'lust for someone' in casual speech when 'attracted to someone' is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is epithumia, meaning strong desire or longing, which can be good or bad depending on its object. In Matthew 5:28 Jesus says that looking at a woman with lustful desire is adultery in the heart. In Galatians 5:16-17 Paul describes the desires of the flesh in conflict with the Spirit. In James 1:14-15 desire is described as conceiving and giving birth to sin.

lust.etymology: From Middle English *lust*, from Old English *lust* (“lust, pleasure, longing”), from **lustu*, from Proto-Germanic **lustuz*.

senses.definition: Wrongdoing.
Misconduct or wrongdoing, especially by a public official and causing damage.

core.definition: Wrongdoing, especially illegal or unethical conduct by a public official while in office that harms the public.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on FEE, the second syllable. The final syllable is a reduced 'uns' sound, not a full 'ance'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names serious misconduct, usually by someone in a position of public trust.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use malfeasance mainly in legal, political, and news contexts, such as describing a city official who misused funds. In everyday speech they would more often say 'corruption' or 'wrongdoing.' It is not used for minor mistakes.

distinctions.note: Misfeasance is the lawful act performed wrongly, while malfeasance is an act that is itself unlawful.
Nonfeasance is failing to do a duty, while malfeasance is actively doing something wrong.
Corruption usually implies bribery or abuse for personal gain. Malfeasance is a broader term for any serious wrongful act by an official.

examples.everyday: People in my town are upset about the mayor's malfeasance, and they're talking about it at every meeting.
examples.professional: Our compliance team must report any suspected malfeasance by vendors to the audit committee within 48 hours.
examples.analytical: Political theorists distinguish between incompetence and malfeasance, arguing that only the latter betrays the public trust.

nuance.analogy: Malfeasance is like a referee who secretly takes money from one team: the rules are broken by the person who is supposed to enforce them.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French malfaisance, from mal 'bad' and faire 'to do.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'mal-fee-ZANCE' with the stress on the last syllable.
Confusing it with malfunction, which refers to machines or systems failing, not wrongdoing by people.

malfeasance.etymology: From Old French *malfaisance*, derived from *malfaire*, *maufaire* (“to do evil”), from Latin *malefaciō* (“to do evil”), from *male* (“evilly”) + *faciō* (“to do, make”).

senses.definition: Corrupt behavior, illegitimate activity, especially by someone in authority.

core.definition: Corrupt or dishonest conduct by a person in authority, especially misuse of public money or office.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SAY, the third syllable, and the middle syllable is a reduced, r-colored vowel. The final -tion is pronounced 'shun', not 'tee-on'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It is a serious accusation of wrongdoing, usually financial or political.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use malversation mainly in legal, governmental, or academic writing, and it is rare in everyday speech. Journalists and lawyers may prefer 'embezzlement', 'corruption', or 'misuse of funds' for clarity. The word is most common in discussions of public officials who misuse office or public money.

distinctions.note: Embezzlement is the specific crime of stealing money entrusted to you, while malversation is a broader term for corrupt conduct in office.
Corruption is the common everyday term, while malversation is more technical and legalistic.

examples.everyday: The news said the city official was under investigation for malversation, which is a fancy way of saying he stole public money.
examples.professional: Our compliance team flagged possible malversation in the contract approvals and referred the case to legal counsel.
examples.analytical: Political theorists distinguish ordinary misconduct from malversation, which involves the abuse of public trust for private gain.

nuance.analogy: Malversation is like a bank teller who quietly takes money from the vault while pretending to follow the rules.
nuance.etymology: From Latin malversatio, from malversari, 'to misbehave', from male, 'badly', plus versari, 'to conduct oneself'.
common_mistakes: Confusing malversation with malnutrition or malfunction because of the shared prefix mal-.
Using malversation for minor mistakes; it implies deliberate corrupt conduct.

malversation.etymology: From French *malversation*, from *malverser*, from Latin *male* *versari* (“behave badly”).

senses.definition: The projection of a joint probability distribution onto one of its component random variables.

core.definition: In statistics, the probability distribution of one variable in a joint distribution, found by summing or integrating over the others.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the second part, byoo, in distribution, and the first word has a secondary stress. Say the r clearly in both words, and remember the reduced vowel in -shun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is used only within probability and statistics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use marginal distribution mainly in statistics, machine learning, and data science courses and papers. Data scientists may say the marginal of x for short. In a meeting, you can say the marginal for feature A and people will understand it as the one-variable view.

distinctions.note: A joint distribution describes two or more variables together, while the marginal describes one variable by itself.
A conditional distribution fixes one variable at a value, while a marginal distribution averages over the other variables.

examples.everyday: My brother asked what a marginal distribution is, so I used a simple table of dice rolls.
examples.professional: We need the marginal distribution of age before we can compare it with the campaign results.
examples.analytical: The marginal distribution of one variable does not reveal the dependence structure captured in the joint distribution.

nuance.analogy: A marginal distribution is like looking at one column of a spreadsheet by itself, ignoring the other columns.
common_mistakes: Confusing marginal distribution with marginal utility, which is an economics term.
Saying the marginal distribution when you mean a conditional distribution.
Using it for the mean of a sample rather than a probability distribution.

senses.definition: Of a probability distribution, such that any derived probability from a set of random samples is distinct and has no information (i.e. "memory") of earlier samples.
Without a memory or memories.

core.definition: In probability, describing a process whose future behavior depends only on its present state, not on how it got there; the exponential distribution is the standard example.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MEM. The ending "-less" is a short "lis", and the middle syllable is reduced to "er".

nuance.connotation: neutral, because it is a precise technical property.
nuance.usage_note: Statisticians and data scientists use this word in modeling, queueing theory, and survival analysis. In everyday speech, Americans would say "forgetful" or "without memory" instead. In technical talks, you may hear "the memoryless property" as a shorthand.

distinctions.note: In ordinary English, memoryless means forgetful; in statistics it has a precise meaning about conditional probability.
Independence concerns separate events; memorylessness is a property of a single distribution over time.

examples.everyday: My coworker's dog seems memoryless, since it greets me like a stranger every morning.
examples.professional: We assumed the failure times were memoryless, so the remaining lifetime estimate does not depend on the age of the server.
examples.analytical: A distribution is memoryless exactly when the probability of surviving an additional interval is independent of how long the process has already survived.

nuance.analogy: A memoryless process is like a coin that does not remember past flips: each toss starts fresh, regardless of earlier results.
nuance.etymology: Memory comes from Latin memoria; -less is an Old English suffix meaning without.
common_mistakes: Using memoryless as a casual word for forgetful in technical writing where the precise sense is required.
Assuming all distributions are memoryless; only the exponential and geometric distributions have this property.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to mereology, a collection of axiomatic first-order theories dealing with parts and their respective wholes.
senses.example: Join is a mereological relation which can be interpreted as union set-theoretically.

core.definition: Relating to mereology, the formal study of part-whole relations and of how parts compose a whole.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the LAH syllable, with a lighter secondary stress on mih-. Many learners stress the first syllable or say the -ogy ending as a long o; in American English the vowel is short, as in LOD-jih-kul.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in philosophy, logic, formal ontology and knowledge representation, mostly in academic writing and technical discussion. You will almost never hear it in casual speech. When you need a everyday phrase, say "about parts and wholes."

distinctions.note: Ontological concerns what kinds of things exist; mereological concerns only how parts relate to wholes, which is one tool within ontology.
Topological concerns continuity and nearness; mereotopology combines both, but mereology alone deals only with parts and wholes.

examples.everyday: We got into a mereological argument at dinner about whether a ship with every plank replaced is still the same ship.
examples.professional: The ontology team needs a mereological model so that the engine and wheels are linked as parts of the car.
examples.analytical: A mereological account of the self treats a person as a fusion of parts, which raises the question of whether any such fusion is ever a person.

nuance.analogy: A mereological theory is like the instruction manual for a LEGO set, explaining how small bricks compose the finished model.
nuance.etymology: From Greek meros (part) and -logy (study of), coined by Stanisław Leśniewski in 1916.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (MER-ee-uh-LAH-jih-kuhl); the main stress falls on the LAH syllable.
Using mereological to mean holistic or ontological in general; it refers specifically to part-whole relations.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or originating from a meteor.
senses.example: meteoric iron

senses.definition: Like a meteor in speed, brilliance, or ephemeralness.
senses.example: Her meteoric rise to power was followed by a slow, lackluster career at the top.

senses.definition: Influenced by the weather.
senses.example: a meteoric flower

senses.definition: Originating in the atmosphere.

core.definition: Extremely fast and brief in success or rise, like a meteor; describing something that rises or falls very quickly.

pronunciation.tip: The strongest stress is on the -OR- syllable, with a weaker stress on mee. The first syllable rhymes with 'see', and the final -ic is a short 'ik'. Many learners stress the first syllable by mistake.

nuance.connotation: positive when describing a rapid rise to success, negative when describing a sudden collapse; context determines the tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use meteoric in news, business, and sports to describe an impressive rise, such as a startup or an athlete's career. It is a little dramatic, so it suits writing and conversation about fame or achievement rather than routine events. For an everyday comparison, Americans may say the rise was 'incredibly fast' instead.

distinctions.note: Rapid is neutral and general; meteoric adds the idea of a brilliant, dramatic rise that is often brief.
Sudden only means happening without warning, while meteoric suggests a fast climb to prominence.

examples.everyday: Her podcast had a meteoric rise after one friend shared it online.
examples.professional: Our product saw meteoric adoption after the new release, so we need to scale the servers quickly.
examples.analytical: The meteoric ascent of certain political movements often hides fragile institutional foundations.

nuance.analogy: Like a shooting star that flashes across the sky and quickly disappears, a meteoric career is bright but can be brief.
nuance.etymology: From meteor, from Greek meteōros, 'high in the air', from meta and eōros, 'raised'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (MEE-tee-OR-ik) rather than the -OR- syllable.
Confusing meteoric with meteorological, which refers to weather.

senses.definition: The mother (founding) polis (city state) of a colony.
A large, busy city, especially as the main city in an area or country or as distinguished from surrounding rural areas.
The see of a metropolitan bishop, ranking above its suffragan diocesan bishops.
A generic focus in the distribution of plants or animals.

core.definition: A very large, busy city, especially the main city of a region or country, in contrast to smaller towns and rural areas.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the first and later syllables are reduced to schwa and short i. The t is a flap, so it sounds like muh-DRAH.

nuance.connotation: neutral to positive. It suggests size, energy, and importance, but it can sound grand or old-fashioned in everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use metropolis for big cities in writing, journalism, and formal speech, such as describing New York or Chicago as a metropolis. In casual conversation, people usually say big city or the city. The word can also sound slightly dramatic, so use it when you want to emphasize scale.

distinctions.note: City is the everyday word for any urban place, while metropolis stresses great size and regional importance.
A metropolitan area is a statistical region including a city and its suburbs, while a metropolis is the large city itself.

examples.everyday: Most of my cousins moved from the farm to the big metropolis after college.
examples.professional: Our sales team covers the whole metropolis, so territories are split by neighborhood.
examples.analytical: Historians describe the medieval metropolis as a center of trade that drew power away from rural manors.

nuance.analogy: A metropolis is like a giant hub in a wheel, with roads and people flowing in from every spoke.
nuance.etymology: From Greek metropolis, mother city, from meter, mother, and polis, city.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the first syllable, as in MET-ruh-polis.
Using metropolis for a small town, where city or town is more natural.
Confusing it with metropolitan, which is the adjective for the big-city area.

metropolis.etymology: Late Latin *mētropolis*, from Ancient Greek *μητρόπολις* (“mother city”), from *μήτηρ* (“mother”) + *πόλις* (“city”).

senses.definition: In a mighty manner.
senses.example: The chivalrous knights entered the lists and fought mightily.

senses.definition: With much physical force, power, or strength; also, with divine or superhuman power or strength.
senses.example: The chivalrous knights entered the lists and fought mightily.

senses.definition: With much emotional, intellectual, or mental force or power; vehemently.
Of a characteristic: provided or present to a powerful or strong extent.
To a great extent; extremely, greatly.
senses.example: He sounded mightily proud of himself.

core.definition: With great force, power, or strength; forcefully and intensely.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MY. The middle syllable is a reduced 'tuh,' and the final -ly sounds like 'lee,' not 'lie.'

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests strength or effort, often in emotional or religious contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mightily for emphasis in a formal or heightened tone, most often in phrases like 'pray mightily,' 'struggle mightily,' or 'work mightily.' In casual talk, 'really' or 'a lot' is more natural. It is common in church and Bible study settings.

distinctions.note: Greatly is everyday and neutral, while mightily adds a sense of strength, effort, or dramatic force.
Strongly is the neutral choice for intensity, while mightily is more dramatic and often literary.

examples.everyday: My son is struggling mightily with his math homework tonight.
examples.professional: The team worked mightily to finish the data migration before the release deadline.
examples.analytical: The author argues that believers must strive mightily, yet all real strength ultimately comes from God.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner pushing the last hundred meters with everything they have left.
nuance.etymology: From Old English mihtig (powerful), from might, with the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'mighty' as an adverb, as in 'worked mighty'; the adverb is 'mightily.'
Stressing the last syllable instead of the first, MY.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture often describes earnest, forceful effort or God's power in these terms. Jonah 3:8 calls the people of Nineveh to cry mightily to God. The Greek word euteneōs, meaning 'vigorously,' appears in Acts 18:28, where Apollos refutes the Jews. Exodus 1:20 notes that God dealt well with the midwives and that the people multiplied and grew very strong.

mightily.etymology: From Middle English *mightili* (“with might, powerfully, strongly; forcefully, violently; greatly; etc.”), from Old English *meahtiglice* (“with might, powerfully, mightily”), from *meahtiġ*, *mihtiġ* (“powerful, mighty”) + *-līċe*.

senses.definition: A search method that estimates the value of moves by playing many random or guided simulations from each position.

core.definition: A game-tree search method that estimates the value of moves by running many random or guided simulated games from each position.

pronunciation.tip: In the phrase, the strongest stress falls on SEARCH. Monte Carlo and tree are lighter, and 'Carlo' is said KAR-loh in American speech. The 'r' in Carlo and in search is pronounced in General American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term used in AI and game research.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in AI, machine learning and game programming, for example when discussing how a chess or Go program chooses moves. It is usually abbreviated as MCTS in papers and code. Most people outside the field will not know it, so explain it briefly.

distinctions.note: Minimax explores the game tree systematically and assumes perfect play; Monte Carlo tree search estimates moves through random simulation.
Monte Carlo simulation is the general technique of random sampling; MCTS applies it to choosing moves in a game tree.

examples.professional: Our game agent uses Monte Carlo tree search, so it improves as we give it more simulation time.
examples.analytical: Monte Carlo tree search balances exploration of untested moves against exploitation of moves that have already performed well, which is a form of the bandit problem.

nuance.analogy: Like a chess player who tries out thousands of quick practice games from each position and keeps the moves that win most often.
nuance.etymology: Monte Carlo is named after the casino district in Monaco, by analogy with chance; tree refers to the branching structure of possible game moves.
common_mistakes: Stressing Monte as the main stress; the strongest stress is on the search term SEARCH.
Using it as a name for any game AI; it refers to a specific search method.

conversation.text: Monte Carlo tree search estimates move values by running many simulated playouts from each position.
The strongest Go programs combine Monte Carlo tree search with deep neural networks that evaluate positions.
Monte Carlo tree search works well when we can simulate cheaply but lack a good evaluation function.

senses.definition: To mix together, to mix up; to confuse.
senses.example: Young children tend to muddle their words.

senses.definition: To mash slightly for use in a cocktail.
senses.example: He muddled the mint sprigs in the bottom of the glass.

senses.definition: To dabble in mud.
To make turbid or muddy.
To think and act in a confused, aimless way.
To cloud or stupefy; to render stupid with liquor; to intoxicate partially.
To waste or misuse, as one does who is stupid or intoxicated.
A mixture; a confusion; a garble.
senses.example: The muddle of nervous speech he uttered did not have much meaning.

senses.definition: A mixture of crushed ingredients, as prepared with a muddler.

core.definition: To confuse or mix things up so that they become disorganized or hard to understand. Also used as a noun for a mix-up.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the second syllable a quick syllabic l with no vowel in between. The word is two syllables, not 'mud-dle' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: negative or mildly negative. It suggests confusion or carelessness, but it is usually lighter than 'mess up.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'muddle' in everyday talk to describe mixed-up papers, schedules, or explanations, as in 'Don't muddle the two accounts.' 'Muddle through' means to manage a difficult situation without a clear plan but still succeed, a common phrase in work and life. The noun 'a muddle' is used in phrases like 'in a muddle' or 'what a muddle.' In a cocktail context it means crushing ingredients lightly, which is a specialized sense.

distinctions.note: Confuse focuses on a person's understanding, while muddle focuses on the disorder of things or ideas that have become tangled.
Mess up is more informal and often implies an error or failure, while muddle suggests mixing or tangling without necessarily causing damage.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I muddled the dates, so we're actually meeting on Thursday, not Wednesday.
examples.professional: The vendor's invoice muddled our budget codes, so finance has to reconcile everything before the audit.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the author muddles moral duty with personal preference, which makes the central argument hard to test.

nuance.analogy: Muddle is like a drawer of tangled cables: each cable is fine alone, but together they become a knot.
nuance.etymology: Probably from mud, in the sense of making something muddy or confused.
common_mistakes: Using 'muddle' only for mixing liquids, when in American English it usually means confusion.
Putting 'through' in the wrong place, as in 'muddle over the problem' instead of 'muddle through the problem.'

muddle.etymology: From Middle English *modelen* (attested in present participle *modeland* (“wallowing”)), from Middle Dutch *moddelen* (“to make muddy”), from *modde*, *mod* (“mud”).

core.definition: A rich but foolish man of Carmel who insulted King David's men and whose wife Abigail saved his household from David's anger.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is reduced, so the ending sounds like 'bul.'

nuance.connotation: negative
nuance.usage_note: In Bible discussion Nabal is a name for a foolish, surly man. Americans may use the Hebrew meaning 'fool' in sermons or teaching, but the word itself is not used in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Fool is a common English word, while Nabal is a proper name that carries the biblical sense of a stubborn, arrogant fool.

examples.everyday: My friend joked that his roommate is a real Nabal when he refuses to share anything with anybody.
examples.professional: In the leadership talk, I used Nabal as the example of a leader who ignores good counsel and endangers his whole team.
examples.analytical: The narrator of 1 Samuel 25 presents Nabal as a rich man whose name, meaning fool, becomes a judgment on his character.

nuance.analogy: Nabal is like the stubborn passenger who refuses the map and then blames everyone for getting lost.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew nabal, 'fool' or 'senseless,' used as a personal name in 1 Samuel 25.
common_mistakes: Treating Nabal as a common noun in everyday speech.
Stressing the second syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Nabal (Hebrew nabal, 'fool') is the husband of Abigail in 1 Samuel 25. He insults David's messengers, and his wife acts quickly to prevent bloodshed. After Nabal's death, ten days later, David marries Abigail. The story shows how wisdom contrasts with folly in 1 Samuel 25:25, where the name is explained by his character.

senses.definition: Emerging; just coming into existence.
Describing the state, aspect, or practice of an abstract concept.
Naissant.

Of the state of an element at the time it is being generated from some compound or transitioning from one state to another; Newly released from a compound (especially hydrogen and oxygen) by a chemical reaction or electrolysis and possessing heightened reactivity; Newly synthesized (especially protein or RNA) by translation or transcription.

core.definition: Just beginning to develop or exist; in an early stage of growth and not yet fully formed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the second syllable a weak schwa. The spelling -scent ends in a t sound, not an s-ent of scent with a clear vowel.

nuance.connotation: positive. It suggests promise and potential, though sometimes with uncertainty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nascent in business writing, journalism and academic prose to describe early-stage markets, movements or ideas. In casual talk people usually say new, early or just starting. Using nascent in ordinary conversation can sound stiff, though it is natural in a presentation.

distinctions.note: Emerging is common in business and suggests something rising into view, while nascent stresses that it is at its very earliest stage.
Embryonic is more literal and biological, while nascent is the common figurative term for early development.

examples.everyday: My sister just started a nascent bakery, so she's still figuring out the recipes and the hours.
examples.professional: We're building tooling for a nascent market, so let's keep the scope small until we see real demand.
examples.analytical: Scholars often treat nascent theories as provisional, since their concepts have not yet been tested against sustained evidence.

nuance.analogy: A nascent idea is like a seedling just breaking through the soil: it is alive and promising, but still fragile.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nascens, present participle of nasci 'to be born'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as NAS-ent, with the first vowel like cat.
Confusing nascent with naive, which means inexperienced or trusting.

nascent.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *nāscēns*, present participle of *nāscor* (“to be born”).

senses.definition: Careless or inattentive.
senses.example: grossly negligent

senses.definition: Culpable due to negligence.
senses.example: prove someone negligent

core.definition: Not giving enough care or attention, so that something bad happens or could happen.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle vowel to a quick 'uh.' The final 'ent' is a weak syllable, sounding like 'jint.'

nuance.connotation: negative, suggesting blame for carelessness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use negligent mostly in legal or formal descriptions, such as 'negligent driver' or 'negligent parent.' In casual speech, 'careless' is more common. Calling a person negligent is a strong criticism, so it can sound harsh in personal conversation.

distinctions.note: Careless is the everyday word for not paying attention; negligent is more formal and often implies responsibility for harm.
Neglectful focuses on failing to look after someone or something over time, especially a child or a responsibility.

examples.everyday: My neighbor was negligent about locking his gate, and his dog got out onto the road.
examples.professional: The contractor was negligent in checking the wiring, so the inspection failed.
examples.analytical: A negligent agent fails to take the precautions that a reasonable person would take in the same circumstances.

nuance.analogy: A negligent driver is like someone who glances at the phone for a second on the highway: nothing seems wrong until something goes badly wrong.
nuance.etymology: From Latin negligens, present participle of neglegere, 'to disregard.'
common_mistakes: Using negligent with 'to' instead of 'in' or 'about': say 'negligent in his duties' or 'negligent about safety.'
Confusing its meaning with 'neglected,' which describes the thing that was not cared for.

negligent.etymology: From Middle English *necligent*, *negligent*, from Old French *negligent*, from Latin *negligēns*.

senses.definition: Reasonably good; almost good; mediocre.
senses.example: What did you think of the guitarist?Not bad, but that solo could have been better.

core.definition: Fairly good or satisfactory, though not outstanding; a casual way to say something is okay or better than expected.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BAD, and 'not' is a short, unstressed-sounding word in fast speech, sounding like 'nah'. Keep the vowel in 'not' as the American open 'ah' sound, the same as in 'cot'.

nuance.connotation: neutral to mildly positive; it can sound like faint praise or understated approval.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'not bad' constantly in small talk, as in 'How's it going?' 'Not bad, how about you?' It can mean fine, okay, or even quite good, depending on tone. A sarcastic or flat tone can mean merely mediocre, so listen to the speaker's voice.

distinctions.note: 'Pretty good' sounds more enthusiastic than 'not bad,' which sounds understated or modest.
'Okay' is a more neutral acceptable level, while 'not bad' often implies slightly better than expected.

collocations: not bad for a first try

examples.everyday: How was your weekend? Not bad, we went hiking and I finally slept in.
examples.professional: The quarterly numbers came in not bad, though we still need to close the gap on customer retention.
examples.analytical: Describing the argument as 'not bad' is a rhetorical hedge: it concedes some merit while withholding full endorsement.

nuance.analogy: Like a B-plus grade, 'not bad' says the result is solid, though not stellar.
common_mistakes: Using 'not bad' in formal praise, where it sounds like faint or grudging approval.
Saying 'no bad' instead of 'not bad.'

conversation.text: "How's it going?" "Not bad. Just a long week."
"How was the movie?" "Not bad. A little long, though."
You made this cake yourself? Not bad at all!

senses.definition: Of or relating to a numen (divinity); indicating the presence of a divinity.
senses.example: His interest in numinous objects led him on a quest for the Holy Grail.

senses.definition: Evoking a sense of the mystical, sublime, or transcendent; awe-inspiring.

core.definition: Evoking a sense of the sacred, mysterious or transcendent, often in a way that inspires awe beyond ordinary understanding.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, NOO. The middle syllable is reduced, so say 'muh' rather than 'mah.' The final -ous is a quiet 'us.'

nuance.connotation: positive. It suggests reverence and wonder, and is used respectfully in religious and philosophical discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mainly use 'numinous' in religious studies, philosophy, literary criticism and serious nature writing. It can sound pretentious in casual talk, so most people would say 'sacred,' 'awe-inspiring' or 'otherworldly' instead. It is most often used to describe places, music or moments of deep quiet.

distinctions.note: Sublime describes awe from vastness or grandeur in nature or art, while numinous specifically points to a sense of the holy or divine.
Mysterious means hard to understand or explain, while numinous adds a religious sense of awe and presence.

examples.everyday: The old stone chapel felt numinous when the choir started singing in the empty room.
examples.professional: The design team wanted the lobby to feel numinous without making visitors feel out of place.
examples.analytical: Rudolf Otto used 'numinous' to name the experience of the holy, which he described as both frightening and fascinating.

nuance.analogy: Like standing at the edge of a canyon in silence: the mind goes quiet and something far larger seems present.
nuance.etymology: From Latin numen, 'divine power', with the English suffix -ous, 'full of'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'numinous' with 'luminous' because of the similar spelling; luminous means bright, while numinous means awe-inspiring.
Using 'numinous' for ordinary beauty; it implies a sense of the sacred or transcendent.

numinous.etymology: From Latin *nūmen* (“nod of the head; divine sway or will; divinity”) *ous*.

senses.definition: Not for publication.
Unofficial.

core.definition: Said or shared in confidence, not for publication, quotation, or official record.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on 'cord' in 'record' as the verb-like second syllable. Pronounce the 'r' clearly in both 'record' and 'off' sound-related syllables, and reduce 'the' to 'thuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It signals confidentiality and can suggest that the speaker is sharing something sensitive or unofficial.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase when speaking to journalists, colleagues, or friends to indicate that what follows should not be quoted or reported. A common phrase before the remark is 'Off the record, I think...' A natural reply is 'Sure, that stays between us.' It is common in politics, business, and news, and it can also be used in everyday conversation.

distinctions.note: On the record means the statement can be quoted and officially recorded; off the record means it cannot.
Confidential describes information that is private or secret; off the record is specifically about not publishing or quoting a remark.

examples.everyday: Off the record, I don't think Jake is going to get the promotion this year.
examples.professional: The director spoke off the record to the reporters, so nothing from the briefing can be quoted.
examples.analytical: Distinguishing on-the-record from off-the-record statements is essential for evaluating how sources shape public narratives.

nuance.analogy: Off the record is like a conversation held behind a closed door, with no transcript kept.
nuance.etymology: From the notion of an official written record, with off meaning outside of it.
common_mistakes: Saying 'out the record', which is not standard; the phrase is 'off the record'.
Using it to mean 'unofficial' only in the sense of informal; it primarily means not for publication.
Pronouncing 'record' as the noun 'REK-ord' when the context needs the verb 'ruh-KORD'.

conversation.text: Off the record, I think the merger is going to happen.
Can I tell you something off the record about the new hire?
The mayor spoke to the reporter off the record.

senses.definition: To perform the functions of some office.
senses.example: She officiated as registrar at the wedding.

senses.definition: To serve as umpire or referee.
senses.example: This is the second time he has officiated at a cup-final.

senses.definition: A person appointed to office, an official.

core.definition: To preside over or referee a ceremony, event, or game, performing the formal duties of that role.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FISH. The 'ci' is pronounced 'shee' and the ending -ate is 'ayt'. Don't turn the middle into 'of-fi-see-ate'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a formal role and carries no judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans commonly say that a pastor officiated a wedding or a referee officiated a game. Using it for ordinary help sounds odd. The noun sense, 'an official,' is rare and mostly found in formal writing.

distinctions.note: Preside means to lead a meeting or group, while officiate means to run a formal ceremony or game according to its rules.
Referee is a specific sports word; officiate is broader and can apply to weddings, funerals, and ceremonies.

examples.everyday: My uncle is going to officiate our wedding, which is a big honor for us.
examples.professional: Two certified referees will officiate the tournament finals next weekend.
examples.analytical: In many traditions, only an ordained minister may officiate at the sacrament, which raises questions about authority.

nuance.analogy: Like a conductor who keeps the orchestra in time: the rules are kept by someone standing in front.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin officiare, to perform a duty, from officium, duty.
common_mistakes: Using it for any kind of help; it is for formal roles such as referee or minister.
Pronouncing the middle vowel as a long i, as in 'of-fi-SIGH-ate'.

senses.definition: In a dangerous, hazardous, or delicate situation; at risk.
senses.example: Ever since he was caught stealing office supplies, he has been on thin ice with his boss.

senses.definition: Dangerously, hazardously, delicately.

core.definition: In a risky situation where one mistake could cause serious trouble or damage.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ICE, with a lighter secondary stress on THIN. Say 'on' as a reduced 'awn' and keep the final s clear in 'ice'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It signals danger, precariousness, or being close to losing favor, a job, or trust.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom for a person whose standing, job, or reputation is at risk after a mistake or a warning. You can say 'He's on thin ice after missing three deadlines.' A natural reply is 'I know, I'll be more careful.' It is informal and works in workplaces, families, and sports.

distinctions.note: In hot water means already in trouble; on thin ice means at risk of trouble if one more thing goes wrong.
On the line means at stake or at risk of loss; on thin ice focuses more on a fragile standing or a precarious situation.

collocations: on thin ice with the boss
on thin ice after the warning

examples.everyday: After missing my cousin's birthday again, I'm definitely on thin ice with my sister.
examples.professional: Marcus has missed two code reviews this sprint, so he's on thin ice with the team lead.
examples.analytical: A regime that relies on fear while losing public trust is always on thin ice, however stable it appears.

nuance.analogy: Like walking across a frozen pond that might crack under the next step.
common_mistakes: Saying 'on a thin ice' with an unnecessary article; the idiom is 'on thin ice'.
Using it for a literal situation of physical ice without the figurative sense; it usually means figurative risk.

on-thin-ice.etymology: Referencing a person skating or walking on a frozen-over body of water, at risk of breaking through and falling into the water.

conversation.text: After missing three classes, he's on thin ice with his professor.
You're on thin ice with that client; don't miss another deadline.
The dog is on thin ice after eating my sandwich.

senses.definition: Having properties which are counterintuitive or difficult to handle.
Having properties that cause unusually bad behavior, especially regarding correctness or performance.
Pertaining to pathology.
Relating to, amounting to, or caused by a physical or mental disorder.

core.definition: Relating to disease; in everyday speech, extreme or compulsive in an unreasonable way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the 'LAH' syllable. The last syllable is weak, so it sounds like 'kul,' and the 'o' sound is the American 'ah.'

nuance.connotation: Negative in everyday use, suggesting extreme or compulsive behavior. Neutral in medical contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say pathological liar or pathological about someone's habits, usually in a critical way. It can sound harsh, so use it carefully. In medical contexts, it simply means relating to disease.

distinctions.note: Pathological implies an extreme, almost clinical condition, while compulsive describes a habit that is hard to control.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a pathological liar, so nobody believes his stories anymore.
examples.professional: The test suite includes a pathological case where the input is empty, which breaks the parser.
examples.analytical: Some philosophers argue that a pathological desire for control can distort ordinary moral judgment.

nuance.analogy: Like a fever: it is a sign that something is wrong with the body, not normal function.
nuance.etymology: From pathology, from Greek pathos, 'suffering,' plus -logia, 'study.'
common_mistakes: Using it to mean 'pathetic,' which is different.
Stressing the first syllable instead of 'LAH.'

core.definition: A priest in the Hebrew Bible, son of Eleazar and grandson of Aaron, known for his zeal against idolatry and his role in Israel's worship and leadership.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FY, as in 'fine'. The middle and last syllables are reduced, so do not say 'fi-NEE-has'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a biblical proper name, though his story of zeal is often discussed seriously.
nuance.usage_note: This is the standard English spelling in the RSV and most modern American Bibles. In church or Bible study, you might say 'Phinehas, son of Eleazar' to identify him. Americans may also refer to him as the priest who acted zealously in Numbers 25.

distinctions.note: Phinees is the Douay-Rheims spelling of the same name; in American church settings, Phinehas is the usual form.

examples.everyday: During Bible study, our pastor mentioned Phinehas, the priest whose zeal in Numbers really surprised the group.
examples.professional: In the sermon outline, Phinehas illustrates zeal for holiness, though the passage must be read carefully in its covenant context.
examples.analytical: Psalm 106 recalls Phinehas's act as righteousness reckoned to him, linking his zeal to the covenant of perpetual priesthood.

nuance.analogy: Phinehas is like a sentinel at the gate of a camp, acting quickly to protect the community from what threatens it.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Pinchas; its meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Stressing the middle syllable, as in 'fi-NEE-has'.
Confusing him with Phinees, which is a different spelling of the same name.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew Pinchas (uncertain meaning) is the name of the priest son of Eleazar and grandson of Aaron. In Numbers 25:7-13 he acts with zeal against Zimri and Cozbi, and God makes a covenant of perpetual priesthood with him. In 1 Samuel 4:11 his name recurs among the sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, who die in battle, and in Judges 20:28 he ministers before the ark during the war with Benjamin.

senses.definition: Go and get someone in your car.

core.definition: To drive to a place and collect someone so you can take them somewhere in your car.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on pick and up. Someone reduces to SUM-wun, and pick up links into pi-KUP when the object is a pronoun like me or him.

nuance.connotation: positive. It describes a helpful, friendly act.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say pick someone up for driving to get a person, such as a friend, a child, or a coworker, and then taking them somewhere. You can say I'll pick you up at seven. A natural reply is Sounds good, or Thanks for picking me up. The phrase does not mean meeting someone romantically in casual talk, though it can have that meaning in some contexts.

distinctions.note: Pick up means to collect someone, while drop off means to take someone to a place and leave them there.
Meet is neutral about transportation, while pick up specifically involves collecting someone, often by car.

collocations: pick me up at the airport
I'll pick you up at seven
pick up the kids from school
pick her up at the station

examples.everyday: Can you pick me up at the airport around six? My flight is running a bit late.
examples.professional: I'll pick up our client from the lobby and bring them to the conference room before the review.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the state should pick up those whom the market has dropped, which raises questions about responsibility and dependence.

nuance.analogy: Picking someone up is like collecting a package at the post office, except the package can talk and expects a ride.
common_mistakes: Saying pick up someone at the place without the object in the right position; the object goes between pick and up in the phrase.
Confusing pick someone up with drop someone off, which means the opposite action.

conversation.text: Can you pick me up from the airport on Friday?
School gets out at three, so I need to pick my son up.
She picked her mom up at the train station.

senses.definition: A light truck with an open cargo bed.

core.definition: A light truck with an open cargo bed behind the cab, used for hauling loads and driving on rough roads.

pronunciation.tip: Americans stress PICK in pickup, and the second word is also stressed, so the phrase has two strong beats. Note that pickup here has the vowel of cup, not the vowel of cop.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a common vehicle, and it can suggest work, rural life or practical use.
nuance.usage_note: Pickup truck is the standard American term, and Americans say it constantly. Shortened forms like pickup or truck are common in conversation. The word pickup alone can also mean a small truck or a shortened form of the phrase in a casual setting.
